#126570. Industry News: SAIR: Accelerating Pharma R&D with AI-Powered Structural Intelligence

📅 02 Sep 2025 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1213 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: SAIR: Accelerating Pharma R&D with AI-Powered Structural Intelligence

📅 02 Sep 2025 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1213 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This summer, SandboxAQ released the Structurally Augmented IC50 Repository (SAIR), the largest dataset of co-folded 3D protein-ligand structures paired with experimentally measured IC₅₀ labels, directly linking molecular structure to drug potency and overcoming a longstanding scarcity in training data.
  • It has been revealed that SAIR is an open-sourced dataset and is publicly available for free under a permissive CC BY 4.0 license, making it immediately actionable for commercial and non-commercial R&D pipelines.
  • Sources indicate that AI and computer-aided design have great potential in dramatically accelerating the development of upcoming drugs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This summer, SandboxAQ released the Structurally Augmented IC50 Repository (SAIR), the largest dataset of co-folded 3D protein-ligand structures paired with experimentally measured IC₅₀ labels, directly linking molecular structure to drug potency and overcoming a longstanding scarcity in training data. This dataset is now available on Hugging Face, and for the first time, researchers have open access to more than 5 million AI‑generated, high‑accuracy protein-ligand 3D structures, each paired with validated empirical binding potency data.

It has been revealed that SAIR is an open-sourced dataset and is publicly available for free under a permissive CC BY 4.0 license, making it immediately actionable for commercial and non-commercial R&D pipelines. More than just a dataset, SAIR is a strategic asset that bridges the long-standing data gap in AI-powered drug design. It empowers pharmaceutical, biotech, and tech‑bio leaders to accelerate R&D, expand target horizons, and supercharge AI models – moving more of the costly, lengthy drug design and optimization from the wet lab to in silico. This means shorter hit‑to‑lead timelines, more efficient lead optimization, fewer dead‑end projects, and a more predictable path from initial idea to clinical candidate.

Sources indicate that AI and computer-aided design have great potential in dramatically accelerating the development of upcoming drugs. For decades, scientists have dreamed about AI that could identify or design a potent, non-toxic, and efficacious compound from a prompt describing the disease pathway, practically compressing years of drug R&D into a few minutes on a computer. However, this vision is bottlenecked by AI's ability to predict critical drug properties like potency, toxicity, etc., based solely on its molecular structure.

Furthermore, traditional structure‑based discovery is often slowed early by the determination of reliable 3D structures. Three‑dimensional molecular structure dictates a molecule’s functionality, dynamics and interactions, which is especially notable when a potential drug candidate is expected to bind to a human protein target.

Sources indicate that experimental methods, such as X-ray crystallography and cryo-EM, require extensive time and investment, and many promising disease targets still lack experimentally validated structural information. Computer simulations have helped lower the barrier of getting 3D structures and predicting binding affinity. However, earlier generations of algorithms for protein folding and docking (like AlphaFold and Vina respectively) only predict static snapshots of molecules and proteins (which, in reality, are inherently dynamic and shape-changing).

SAIR solves that constraint by compiling over 1 million unique computationally co-folded protein–ligand pairs, ultimately yielding 5.24 million distinct 3D complexes (five different co-folded structures per pair). Each structure is paired with a curated IC₅₀ measurement from ChEMBL or BindingDB, providing for the first time a scalable link between high-quality 3D structures and drug potency, and bridging the historic data gap that has hindered AI-driven discovery. Deep-learned affinity models such as Boltz-2, trained on similar data, have been shown to yield up to a 1,000x speed-up over the traditional, first-principle approach.

In a recent development, creating SAIR was a major feat of high-performance AI computing. It took more than 130,000 GPU hours to compute the SAIR dataset using Boltz1, a cofolding AI model, on a cluster of 760 NVIDIA H100 processors, leveraging the NVIDIA DGX Cloud through Google Cloud Platform.

Capturing highly granular node, operator, scheduler, and GPU metrics, as well as a close collaboration on both infrastructure and workload optimization, helped NVIDIA AI Accelerator and SandboxAQ engineering teams identify bottlenecks and optimize configurations to achieve the highest workload throughput.

Consequently, the two teams were able to achieve > 95% GPU compute utilization for generating the SAIR dataset. This enabled us to create SAIR in three weeks – as opposed to the original estimate of three months (more than a 4X speed up) – and resulted in a highly optimized, GPU-native computational workflow that seamlessly integrates with today’s cutting-edge enterprise compute environments.

Generating such a massive volume of data is only half the story. Equally vital is confidence in its quality, which is why every predicted complex underwent rigorous validation with PoseBusters, an industry-standard, open-source tool for benchmarking structure-related AI in drug discovery. This tool checks chemical sanity and physical plausibility.

The end result was that 97 percent of SAIR’s structures passed all checks. In addition to PoseBusters validation, we benchmarked leading affinity prediction methods, such as empirical scoring functions, 3D CNNs, and graph neural networks, across SAIR’s synthetic structures and experimental IC₅₀ values. The detailed results of these studies are available in our scientific manuscript on bioRxiv.

SAIR data is a reliable foundation for benchmarking newly introduced models as well as downstream modelling, screening, and design.

A persistent challenge in drug discovery is the “dark proteome,” or disease‑relevant proteins for which experimental structures simply do not exist. SAIR illuminates these uncharted regions by providing credible, AI‑predicted complexes wherever experimental data is scarce. For example, more than 40 percent of the proteins in the SAIR dataset have no available structures in the Protein Data Bank (PDB) whatsoever, with or without a ligand. SAIR addresses one of the biggest challenges with existing AI models, low generalizability due to data scarcity. With SAIR, scientists can now explore targets that were previously deemed undruggable, armed with structural hypotheses to guide virtual screening and lead optimization using trustworthy model predictions.

Sources indicate that moreover, SAIR’s cross‑target breadth uncovers polypharmacology patterns and elucidates how a single molecule might interact with multiple proteins. Leveraging this rich tapestry of interactions, you can train AI models to predict off‑target effects or identify upcoming repurposing opportunities, equipping your organization with a deeper understanding of compound profiles before any lab work begins.

SAIR is freely available on Hugging Face. Here’s a quick guide to pull SAIR from Hugging Face, peek at the main table, and (optionally) download a few structure archives.

We use the Hub to fetch files and pandas+pyarrow to read the Parquet.

This grabs the file from the Hub and loads it into a DataFrame.

Structure files are shipped as many .tar.gz archives under structures_compressed/. List them and pick what you need.

Each archive can be large (≈10 GB). Download only the ones you need and extract them locally.

Recent findings suggest that A full version of this script, including more robust logging and validation, is available in the README file for your convenience. For more details, visit the SAIR homepage, read our manuscript on bioRxiv, or watch our 25-minute joint webinar with NVIDIA, where we demonstrate SAIR and explain how data is structured within it. Extensive documentation, tutorials, and example benchmarks are available to facilitate its use and accelerate internal adoption.The future of drug discovery is data-driven, AI-accelerated, and grounded in scalable, high-quality structural insights. While we don’t yet have AI that can design effective drug therapies with just a prompt, SAIR brings researchers ever closer to that goal with fresh data and insights that can potentially shave years from even AI-accelerated R&D pipelines.We can’t wait to see what researchers will build using SAIR, and SandboxAQ experts are here to support them throughout the discovery process.

Contact the authors or post on the SAIR dataset discussion page.

Authors: Arman Zaribafiyan, Georgia Channing, Zane Beckwith, and Rudi Plesch.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A Finnish study has found an unexpected association between screen use and cognitive performance.
  • Industry observers note that low levels of physical activity among adolescents remain a significant public health concern.
  • Industry observers note that these years are especially crucial because the brain is still developing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A Finnish study has found an unexpected association between screen use and cognitive performance. Children who accumulated more screen time as they grew up tended to show better cognitive processing during adolescence. One of the researchers cautions against viewing screen time as entirely harmful and indicates the goal should be to balance physical activity with screen use that encourages active thinking.

Industry observers note that low levels of physical activity among adolescents remain a significant public health concern. Sedentary behavior has been associated with poorer academic achievement, while physical activity is known to support brain function, particularly in adults. Much less is known, however, about how physical activity and sedentary behavior during childhood and adolescence relate to cognitive processing later in adolescence.

Industry observers note that these years are especially crucial because the brain is still developing. Factors that shape cognitive abilities during childhood and adolescence may have lasting effects that extend into adulthood, potentially influencing education and working life.

Researchers examined how physical activity, sedentary behavior, and screen time from childhood through adolescence were related to cognitive processing in the teenage years. They also looked for differences between girls and boys and investigated whether the intensity of physical activity played a role.

More Screen Time Linked to Better Cognitive Processing.

The results showed that greater screen time beginning in childhood was associated with better cognitive processing in adolescence.

"The findings suggest that screen time can support children's and adolescents' cognitive processing. Presumably, the essential point here is what kind of things they do in their screen time. Teachers and parents should encourage children to use devices and screens in such ways that promote active thinking, problem-solving, creativity and learning," states Doctoral Researcher Petri Jalanko from the University of Jyväskylä.

The findings suggest that the type of screen activity may be important. Digital activities that involve learning, creativity, problem-solving, or other forms of active mental engagement could potentially help explain the association observed in the study.

"We should not regard screen time solely as harmful but seek balance between physical activity and screen time that promotes active thinking," Jalanko summarizes.

Physical Activity Showed Different Links in Girls and Boys.

The relationship between physical activity and cognition was more complicated.

Among girls, greater amounts of light intensity physical activity since childhood were associated with better working memory during adolescence. Among boys, greater participation in guided physical activity from childhood through adolescence was linked to better working memory.

The researchers also found an unexpected pattern involving unsupervised exercise. Lower levels of self-reported unsupervised physical activity were associated with better cognitive processing in adolescence.

Recent findings suggest that by contrast, physical activity and sedentary time measured using a device that tracked heart rate and movement were not associated with cognitive processing. One possible explanation is that these sensors can measure movement and physiological activity but cannot determine exactly what a person is doing during periods of activity or inactivity.

Industry observers note that "Our study indicates that the connections of physical activity and sedentary behavior to cognitive processing are complex and depend on the sex, the type and assessment method of physical activity and sedentary time. Moreover, boys and girls may benefit from different types of physical activity in view of brain health," Jalanko adds.

More Research Is Needed to Determine Cause and Effect.

The researchers emphasize that the findings show associations rather than proving that screen time or particular types of physical activity directly cause changes in cognitive performance.

"However, we need more intervention studies to find out causal relations and sex differences in this respect. Moreover, it is important to examine more specifically the effects of the intensity of physical activity on changes taking place in cognitive processing.".

Recent findings suggest that the results come from an eight-year follow-up of the PANIC study on children's physical activity and nutrition. The current analysis included 124 girls and 136 boys with an average age of 15.8 years.

It has been revealed that researchers measured physical activity and sedentary behavior using both survey questionnaires and a device that combined heart rate and movement measurements. Learning, attention, and working memory were evaluated using the CogState test battery.

The research was published in the journal Pediatric Exercise Science.

The alerts caught a total of 54 candidates, with 111 total when combined with other means, The Korean Herald reports.

The government even requests public institutions and private companies start work later, delaying the rush hour and ensuring the students arrive unimpeded.

The confession went live days before the Suneung, prompting the South Korean government to tighten up its anti-cheating measures for the exam, with Prime Minister Lee Jae Myung stating, "Cheating involving the abuse of AI in South Korea, where public examinations significantly affect the distribution of opportunities and resources, rocks the basic order of our society by undermining fairness and trust," calling for an overhaul of the system to address AI-assisted cheating, as reported by Yonhap News Agency.

Industry observers note that the first alert rang at 8:30 AM, ten minutes before the exam started, catching 31 students with unauthorized devices, whose scores were immediately invalidated despite the test not having started yet. The next two alerts at 2:21 and 2:57 PM caught 23 more, bringing the total to 54. As of today, Yonhap News Agency reports that 111 total students were caught with unauthorized devices — 52 were caught through other methods such as metal detectors, WiFi signal detection, and physical inspections, with a further five caught red-handed using prohibited devices.

According to recent reports, alongside the South Korean government’s reaction to the confession, a law school entrance exam candidate accused of AI-assisted cheating like Han Won-seok had died on the day of the Suneung. Months later, he published a book about his study methods, talking about lifestyle changes, exercise, diet, and even reduced smartphone use.

Tiny robots powered by light can hunt down and collect bacteria

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Robots small enough to operate in the microbial world could give scientists a latest way to directly handle objects that are impossible to manipulate by hand.
  • That capability could be especially useful for biological materials in water, including individual cells and bacteria.
  • In a recent development, one of the biggest obstacles in developing machines this small is finding an effective way to propel and control them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Robots small enough to operate in the microbial world could give scientists a latest way to directly handle objects that are impossible to manipulate by hand. These tiny machines are around 50 times smaller than the diameter of a human hair, bringing researchers closer to the long-pursued goal of interacting directly with the microscopic world.

That capability could be especially useful for biological materials in water, including individual cells and bacteria. Precisely controlling and moving objects at this scale has been a persistent challenge. The newly developed nanorobots show that it is already possible to collect bacteria, transport them, and release them at selected locations.

Light Powers and Steers the Tiny Robots.

In a recent development, one of the biggest obstacles in developing machines this small is finding an effective way to propel and control them. At Julius-Maximilians-Universität Würzburg (JMU), a research team led by Professor Bert Hecht has been developing a solution that uses the recoil produced by individual photons to move microscopic devices known as microdrones.

The devices contain as many as four plasmonic nanoantennas. These antennas absorb light with a particular color and helicity, then emit that light in a specific direction. Redirecting each photon creates a tiny recoil force, similar in principle to the recoil produced when a bullet is fired. Because the microdrones have so little mass, those extremely small forces can generate substantial acceleration and speed.

Sources indicate that for the latest work, the researchers reduced the size of their light-powered robots even further, producing devices smaller than one micrometer. Simplifying the steering system was an important part of achieving that size while retaining propulsion based on photon recoil.

According to recent reports, the new control method takes advantage of nanoscale antenna wires built into the robot. These wires naturally tend to align with the polarization direction of incoming light. By changing the light's polarization, the researchers can control which direction the nanorobot faces. At the same time, photon recoil continues to propel it forward, creating a steering system that works somewhat like the directional control used in larger vehicles.

Nanorobots Act as "Microscopic Cleaners".

"In essence, we have built a light-driven nanorobot that can track down and collect bacteria," indicates Jin Qin, lead experimental scientist of the study. "By simplifying the design, we reached a size at which these robots can operate directly in the microbial world - almost like microscopic cleaning devices.".

According to recent reports, the robots are also highly maneuverable. They can make extremely fast 90° turns, helping them scan broad areas of a sample in an organized and efficient way. They can also selectively capture, carry, and release substantial numbers of bacteria.

According to recent reports, under controlled laboratory conditions, this means the nanorobots can effectively "clean" microscopic environments. They gather bacteria from one area and deposit them at specifically chosen locations.

"This is a striking example of how light can be used not only to observe the microscopic world, but also to actively shape it," adds Bert Hecht. "The idea of tiny robotic cleaners may sound futuristic, but we are already demonstrating the physical principles that make it possible.".

The robots remain fully maneuverable even while carrying larger groups of bacteria, although their speed decreases somewhat under the added load. That ability to keep functioning while transporting larger bacterial clusters points to possible future uses in microbiology, biomedical research, and precise manipulation of materials at the microscopic scale.

Welcome EmbeddingGemma, Google's latest efficient embedding model

📅 04 Sep 2025 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2710 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today, Google releases EmbeddingGemma, a state-of-the-art multilingual embedding model perfect for on-device use cases.
  • According to recent reports, text embeddings have become the backbone of modern natural‑language applications, turning words, sentences, and documents into dense vectors that capture meaning, sentiment, and intent.
  • Sources indicate that building on this foundation, Google DeepMind’s EmbeddingGemma arrives as the newest, most capable small multilingual embedding model yet.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, Google releases EmbeddingGemma, a state-of-the-art multilingual embedding model perfect for on-device use cases. Designed for speed and efficiency, the model features a compact size of 308M parameters and a 2K context window, unlocking new possibilities for mobile RAG pipelines, agents, and more. EmbeddingGemma is trained to support over 100 languages and is the highest-ranking text-only multilingual embedding model under 500M on the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB) at the time of writing.

According to recent reports, text embeddings have become the backbone of modern natural‑language applications, turning words, sentences, and documents into dense vectors that capture meaning, sentiment, and intent. These vectors enable fast similarity search, clustering, classification, and retrieval across massive corpora, powering everything from recommendation engines and semantic search to retrieval-augmented generation and code‑search tools. Embedding models that calculate these embeddings are widely used, with well over 200 million monthly downloads on Hugging Face.

Sources indicate that building on this foundation, Google DeepMind’s EmbeddingGemma arrives as the newest, most capable small multilingual embedding model yet. With just 308M parameters, a 2k‑token context window, and support for over 100 languages, EmbeddingGemma delivers state‑of‑the‑art performance on the Massive Multilingual Text Embedding Benchmark (MMTEB) while staying under 200 MB of RAM when quantized.

The various design choices result in a very practical, open-source tool for computing high-quality multilingual embeddings on everyday devices.

In this blogpost, we describe the EmbeddingGemma architecture and training, and show you how to use the model with various frameworks like Sentence Transformers, LangChain, LlamaIndex, Haystack, txtai, Transformers.js, Text Embedding Inference, and ONNX.

It has been revealed that afterwards, we demonstrate how to finetune EmbeddingGemma on your domain for even stronger performance. In our example, we finetune EmbeddingGemma on the Medical Instruction and Retrieval Dataset (MIRIAD). The resulting model, sentence-transformers/embeddinggemma-300m-medical, achieves state-of-the-art performance on our task: retrieving passages of scientific medical papers in response to detailed medical questions. It even outperforms models twice as significant on this task.

It has been revealed that embeddingGemma builds on the Gemma3 transformers backbone, but modified to use bi-directional attention instead of causal (one-way) attention. This means that earlier tokens in the sequence can attend to later tokens, effectively turning the architecture from a decoder into an encoder. Encoder models can outperform LLMs, which are decoders, on embedding tasks like retrieval (Weller et al., 2025). With this backbone, the model can process a sizable 2048 tokens at once, sufficient for typical retrieval inputs, especially given that larger inputs often result in information loss in the text embeddings.

In a recent development, beyond the new Gemma3-based encoder backbone, which produces token embeddings, a mean pooling layer converts these token embeddings into text embeddings. Lastly, two dense layers transform the text embeddings into their final form, a 768-dimensional vector.

In a recent development, the EmbeddingGemma model has been trained with Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL), allowing you to truncate the 768‑dimensional output to 512, 256, or 128 dimensions on demand. This results in faster downstream processing and lower memory and disk space utilization. See the Sentence Transformers usage for a snippet showing how to perform this truncation.

The model has been trained using a carefully curated, multilingual corpus totalling approximately 320 billion tokens. The proprietary dataset is a blend of publicly available web text, code and technical documentation, and synthetic task‑specific examples. It has been filtered to avoid Child Sexual Abuse Material (CSAM), sensitive data, and low-quality or unsafe content.

EmbeddingGemma was benchmarked on the MMTEB (Multilingual, v2) and MTEB (English, v2) suites, which span a wide range of tasks, domains, and languages. Despite its modest 308M‑parameter size, the model consistently beats comparable baselines while keeping a very small memory footprint.

The results will be listed on the official MTEB Leaderboard. We exclude any model that has been trained on more than 20% of the MTEB data, to mitigate potential over‑fitting.

The demo can also be experienced in full screen.

Experience the demo yourself on a Desktop device.

EmbeddingGemma is integrated with many popular tools, making it easy to incorporate into your existing workflows and applications. The model has been integrated in Sentence Transformers, and thus also in projects that use Sentence Transformers behind the scenes, such as LangChain, LlamaIndex, Haystack, and txtai. See the examples below to get started with your preferred framework.

For production deployments, you can use Text Embeddings Inference (TEI) to serve the model efficiently on various hardware configurations, and you can use Transformers.js for use in web applications.

Sources indicate that regardless of your framework choice, you should be mindful of the prompts. It has been revealed that because google/embeddinggemma-300m was trained with MRL, the embeddings generated by this model can be truncated to lower dimensionalities without considerably hurting the evaluation performance. Embeddings with lower dimensionalities are both cheaper to store on disk and in memory, as well as faster for downstream tasks like retrieval, clustering, or classification.

In Sentence Transformers, you can set a lower dimensionality using the truncate_dim parameter on either the SentenceTransformer initialization or when calling model.encode/model.encode_query/model.encode_document:.

You can easily deploy EmbeddingGemma for both development and production using Text Embeddings Inference (TEI) version 1.8.1 or later.

If you run the Docker container with the cuda-1.8.1 tag, it includes support for multiple GPU architectures: Turing, Ampere, Ada Lovelace, and Hopper. For a lighter image tailored to just your GPU, you can instead use a specific tag such as turing-1.8.1, 1.8.1 and 86-1.8.1 (Ampere), 89-1.8.1 (Ada Lovelace), or hopper-1.8.1.

Once deployed, regardless of the device or runtime, you can leverage the /v1/embeddings endpoint based on the OpenAI Embeddings API Specification to generate embeddings.

Alternatively, you can also leverage the /embed endpoint from the Text Embeddings Inference Embeddings API, which supports the prompt_name parameter, meaning there’s no need to manually prepend the prompt to the inputs but select it via prompt_name instead.

Additionally, note that since google/embeddinggemma-300m was trained with Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL), you can also leverage the dimensions parameter, on both /v1/embeddings and /embed, to truncate the embeddings to lower dimensionalities (512, 256, and 128) without hurting the evaluation performance.

You can also run the model directly with ONNX Runtime, making it highly portable and cross-platform compatible. The example below demonstrates usage in Python, but the same approach can be applied in other languages (Java, C#, C++, etc.) as well.

As with all models compatible with the Sentence Transformers library, EmbeddingGemma can be easily fine-tuned on your specific dataset. To showcase this, we'll be finetuning google/embeddinggemma-300m on the Medical Instruction and RetrIeval Dataset (MIRIAD) dataset, such that our finetuned model becomes particularly adept at finding passages up to 1000 tokens from scientific medical papers given detailed medical questions. These passages can be used as crucial context for a generative model to answer questions more effectively.

Sources indicate that below, you can explore each key component of the finetuning process using expandable tabs. Each tab contains the relevant code and a detailed explanation.

This code loads the EmbeddingGemma model from Hugging Face, with optional model card metadata for documentation and sharing. The SentenceTransformer class loads the model weights and configuration, while the model_card_data argument attaches metadata useful for inclusion in the automatically generated model card.

This code loads the MIRIAD dataset, or rather, a copy that has been divided into train, eval, and test splits. Using a large, high-quality dataset ensures the model learns meaningful representations, while subsetting allows for faster experimentation. The load_dataset function fetches the dataset from Hugging Face Datasets, and the .select() method limits the number of samples for each split.

Industry observers note that this code defines the loss function for training, using Cached Multiple Negatives Ranking Loss (CMNRL). CMNRL is effective for retrieval tasks, as it uses in-batch negatives to efficiently train the model to distinguish between correct and incorrect pairs. The loss takes question-answer pairs and treats other answers in the batch as negatives, maximizing the distance between unrelated pairs in the embedding space. The mini_batch_size parameter controls the memory usage, but does not affect the training dynamics.

It's recommended to use this loss with a large per_device_train_batch_size in SentenceTransformerTrainingArguments and a low mini_batch_size in CachedMultipleNegativesRankingLoss for a strong training signal with low memory usage. Additionally, the NO_DUPLICATES batch sampler is recommended to avoid accidental false negatives.

This code sets up all hyperparameters and configuration for training, evaluation, and logging. Proper training arguments are crucial for efficient, stable, and reproducible training. The arguments control batch sizes, learning rate, mixed precision, evaluation and saving frequency, and more. Notably, the prompts dictionary maps dataset columns to prompts used by the model to distinguish queries from documents.

This code sets up an evaluator for information retrieval, using queries and a corpus to measure model performance. Evaluation during training helps monitor progress and avoid overfitting. The evaluator computes retrieval metrics (NDCG, MRR, Recall, Precision, MAP, etc.) by checking if the model retrieves the correct passages for each query. It can be run before, during, and after training, and the results will be logged and incorporated in the automatically generated model card.

Note that this snippet in particular uses all (1k) evaluation questions against a corpus of all (1k) evaluation passages and 30k training passages, for a total of 31k documents. Evaluating only against evaluation passages is too simple for the model.

This code initializes and runs the training loop, coordinating all components.

Another week has climaxed and I'm so sorry you had to read that on a Saturday morning. But here we are again, with our regular feature, where we talk about what we've been playing in order that you do too. This week, Marie has been staring at monster butts; Connor has capitulated to World of Warcraft; Kelsey is discovering the joys of a beloved Zelda game for the first time; and Bertie enjoys someone being punched in the face, because I guess he's that sort of person?

Recent findings suggest that but enough about us, what about you? What have you been playing this week? Do tell all! And don't forget we have an entire archive of previous What We've Been Playings for your leisurely perusal, just in case you forgot what you were playing a year or a month or a week ago. And now onward!

Sources indicate that my favourite thing so far about Ocarina of Time is the judgement plastered on little Link's face when he encounters, well, almost everyone. Whether he means to or not, he serves sass all over town, and in Kakariko Village, and I am very much here for it.

Also, I wasn't prepared to come face-to-face with a monster's butt cheeks. At all. Imagine the scene: I'm enjoying the tunes of the Lost Woods, processing the changes that have happened to Hyrule in the last seven years, all while making my way to the Forest Temple. Then the Moblin's turn their backs to reveal... Well, everything.

It has been revealed that this week I've spent an ungodly amount of time playing World of Warcraft: Forever (you may have read my preview on the website) and have been essentially glued to it during every minute of free time I've had away from work. I've got both my main professions above the level 225 mark and I'm firmly in the thick of it now. Levels take longer, items are actually getting good, and I've had to make a second alt character for extra bank space.

Sources indicate that as a result, I've not been to the gym in a while. I actually got one of those emails asking why I've fallen off, offering some tips to get back into the routine. Sorry Nuffield Health, my sleep schedule is ruined and I've substituted proper workouts for squats and basic at-home cardio. Surely, this can't go wrong...

I don't have the same level of nostalgia for Ocarina of Time that my peers do, but that has not stopped me from enjoying every minute of running around Hyrule smashing pots and trying not to cry over the touching cutscenes and, well, Saria.

The game feels like Dark Souls for children (endearing) and that is completely my jam. It's magical, satisfying, and often sad. There's creepy enemies as well as cute ones, trap floors and doors, mysterious NPCs... and my heart just feels so warm whenever I'm playing it. My fingers are now crossed that there's a Majora's Mask remake in the pipeline over at Nintendo. (As well as a Super Mario 64 remake, which I admit, is pushing it. But for what it’s worth, I'd probably sell my soul to see it get the Ocarina treatment.).

In a recent development, it takes me a while to settle with games; it takes me a while to settle full stop. I suppose in Fire Emblem's case I'm out of touch, seeing as the last instalment I played was on 3DS. But I struggled with the garish enthusiasm early on and the whole thing seemed overly simple. Nevertheless, I've settled a bit now, and now that the game's layering on more strategy and Intelligent System's expertise is coming to the fore, I'm beginning to enjoy myself much more.

In a recent development, I wasn't expecting it to be quite so boobsy, though. Was Fire Emblem always this way? Perhaps it's my fault for picking the scantily clad queen Theodora, though that sort of presentation isn't reserved only for her. She's no wallflower, though. My favourite moment so far was when she got off her elephant during a parade - yes, her elephant - and walked over to punch a teenage boy in the face for halting proceedings. Apparently she was doing him a favour.

With 250+ client engagements across both agency and embedded in-house roles, Vitalii Khomenko has seen product teams from the inside in a way few designers have. Here he makes the case for a newly introduced kind of design workflow built for the AI era, and explains why the window to adapt is narrower than most founders think.

In a recent development, for the last decade, every startup conversation about speed eventually became a conversation about engineering. Hiring more developers, cutting scope, choosing a simpler stack, it was almost always a dev-side problem. Vitalii Khomenko, Principal Designer at Orizon Design and founder of Fluente LLC, argues that's no longer true. And he has a specific view on what teams should do instead.

Industry observers note that what makes Khomenko's perspective worth taking seriously isn't just seniority. It's the specific shape of his experience. Over a career spanning 250+ client engagements, he has worked both as an external specialist brought in to deliver and as an embedded designer who became the single connective thread between product, brand, and execution. That dual vantage point is rare. Most designers live on one side of that line. Khomenko has operated extensively on both, which gives him an unusually clear read on where friction actually originates inside product teams, and where it doesn't.

Industry observers note that his work spans early-stage startups finding their first visual language and established brands managing complex, multi-disciplinary design systems. Across that range, certain patterns repeat. And the pattern that started becoming impossible to ignore this year pointed him toward a conclusion that is reshaping how he thinks a modern design workflow should actually be structured.

In a recent development, the bottleneck didn't disappear. It moved. And the workflow needs to move with it.

According to recent reports, when shipping code was slow, the existing design workflow made sense. Multiple rounds of revision, user testing, iteration, all of that fit naturally into the window while engineering caught up. That window is now gone, and most design workflows were never updated to reflect it.

Recent findings suggest that "Founders are asking design teams to move at the same speed as an AI-assisted dev pipeline, and design doesn't compress the same way code does," Khomenko states. The result is a workflow that was built around a constraint that no longer exists, applied to a pipeline that has fundamentally changed around it.

The forced choice between polish and speed that product teams are now navigating isn't fresh as a concept. What's new is how stark it has become, and how directly it traces back to a workflow problem rather than a people problem. "Because development is cheap and fast now, there's constant pressure to ship the next thing immediately," he explains. "But the products that actually retain customers are still the ones where the details were considered carefully. Fewer revision rounds isn't a process improvement if it means shipping avoidable friction.".

Khomenko has watched this play out across enough teams, at enough stages, to be specific about where the existing workflow breaks down. The concern isn't design judgment. It's where that judgment sits in the process, and what format it's expected to produce at the end.

Recent findings suggest that to understand Khomenko's proposed fix, it helps to understand exactly where the current workflow stalls. For most product teams, the end of the design process looks like this: a designer produces polished, dev-ready screens inside Figma, and hands that file to engineering. Engineering then interprets those screens, translates the visual decisions into code, and builds from there.

In a recent development, that translation step, Figma file to working code, is where the pipeline now breaks down. AI-assisted engineering has made the building part dramatically faster. But the translation step hasn't changed. An engineer still has to read a Figma file, interpret spacing, extract assets, make judgment calls about component structure, and write the implementation from scratch. That process takes the same amount of time it always did.

"The manual workflow inside Figma simply isn't keeping up with AI-boosted engineering," Khomenko says. "The design handoff is quietly becoming the thing everyone is waiting on.".

The result is a pipeline where everything around the handoff has accelerated, and the handoff itself has become the single point of drag. Figma, in other words, was built for a world where engineering was the slow part. It wasn't designed to feed a pipeline where engineering moves at AI speed.

This is the core of what Khomenko is proposing, and it's a more significant structural shift than it might first appear.

In his workflow, Figma doesn't disappear. It moves. Rather than serving as both the exploration environment and the final delivery artifact, Figma becomes the visual exploration layer exclusively: the place where brand identity is established, layout logic is worked through, and design direction is validated. It remains the right tool for figuring out what something should look and feel like.

But the final delivery, the artifact that actually goes to engineering, is code. Specifically, components built into prepared libraries that engineering can work from and scale directly, without any translation step in between.

Recent findings suggest that the difference in implementation speed is the point. When a designer delivers a coded component library rather than a Figma file, engineering doesn't need to interpret anything. The decisions are already expressed in the language they're building in. What previously required an engineer to read, interpret, and re-create from a visual reference now arrives ready to use. In a pipeline running on AI-assisted development, that difference compounds fast.

"Figma is still the right place to explore what something should look and feel like," Khomenko says. "But handing over a Figma file and asking engineering to implement it is now the slow path. Delivering in code is the fast path. That's the shift.".

Recent findings suggest that executing this workflow requires a different kind of designer, and Khomenko is direct about that. The UI/UX designer becoming a Design Engineer is, in his assessment, not a distant possibility. It is a matter of time, and the teams treating it as a future consideration rather than a present reality are the ones most likely to find themselves stuck at the handoff.

Recent findings suggest that but Khomenko is equally clear about what this shift doesn't mean. Delivering in code is one part of the role, not the whole of it. The full design cycle isn't going anywhere. Applying branding to imagery, producing animations, building marketing materials, these remain essential creative tasks that require a broad and varied toolkit well beyond code. "The designer of the near future isn't just generating code," he says. "They're moving across the full cycle, brand, motion, marketing, product, with design engineering as an key and growing part of that stack, not a replacement for it.".

What changes is that code-ready delivery becomes a core expectation within that stack. The designer who can move fluidly from visual exploration in Figma to component delivery in code, while also carrying the brand thinking, motion, and marketing creativity that differentiates products at the surface level owners actually experience, is the profile that the upcoming workflow demands.

According to recent reports, khomenko is candid that no single version of this workflow has fully standardized yet. Every team is figuring it out differently. The tools are evolving, the handoff expectations are shifting, and the processes teams are building around all of it vary considerably. There is no off-the-shelf playbook.

But this is precisely where his 250+ engagements become more than a credential. They're a dataset. Having watched enough teams, at enough stages, through enough cycles of tooling change, Khomenko can see through the noise of individual variation and identify what's directionally true even when the specifics are still in flux. "Each team's workflow is really custom at this stage," he states. "But some general patterns of how this is going to look in the near future are already visible.".

Those patterns consistently point in the same direction: design judgment moving earlier, final delivery moving into code, and the designer's role expanding in technical range while staying broad in creative scope. The exact tools and sequences will keep shifting. The underlying logic of the workflow Khomenko is describing is already taking shape in the teams paying closest attention.

For founders and product leads, the workflow Khomenko is describing has direct implications for how teams are staffed, budgeted, and structured.

Front-load design judgment. The biggest leverage in the newly introduced workflow isn't faster execution, it's better problem definition before generation starts. Bring senior design thinking in earlier, when it can shape what gets built rather than polish what's already done.

Recent findings suggest that separate exploration from delivery. Figma and the visual exploration phase serve a distinct purpose from the final delivery layer. Treat them as separate stages with separate expectations, rather than collapsing them into a single step expected to produce everything.

Shift the delivery expectation to code. Whether that means hiring for Design Engineer range, developing it internally, or restructuring handoffs, the end of the design pipeline needs to arrive in a form engineering can work from directly. The translation step is where time goes to die, and it's now the most avoidable part of the process.

Protect the full creative stack. Design engineering matters more than it ever has. It is not, however, the whole job. Teams that reduce design to code generation will lose the brand thinking, motion, and marketing creativity that differentiates products at the surface level users actually experience.

Stay flexible. The workflow is still forming. Teams that build rigidity into their process now will find themselves redoing that work within a year. The teams getting this right are the ones building enough adaptability into their structures to absorb what's still coming.

Industry observers note that "The Figma handoff made sense when engineering was the slow part," Khomenko indicates. "Engineering isn't the slow part anymore. Delivering in code isn't the future of design workflow. For the teams paying attention, it's already the present.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • DNA serves as the genetic blueprint for every living organism, but it is also an extraordinarily dense way to store information.
  • The challenge has been finding a way to make biological DNA function effectively alongside electronic materials.
  • According to recent reports, the work, published in Advanced Functional Materials and the subject of a patent application, relies on two key components.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

DNA serves as the genetic blueprint for every living organism, but it is also an extraordinarily dense way to store information. A single gram can hold about 215 million gigabytes of data. Bringing that remarkable storage capacity into electronics could lead to more efficient data centers, faster processing and systems capable of handling increasingly complex information.

The challenge has been finding a way to make biological DNA function effectively alongside electronic materials. Penn State researchers have now developed an approach designed to overcome that incompatibility.

According to recent reports, the work, published in Advanced Functional Materials and the subject of a patent application, relies on two key components. One is synthetic DNA, made from commercially available, chemically engineered molecules arranged into short genetic sequences tailored for specific electronic requirements. The other is crystalline perovskite, a semiconductor already used in technologies including solar cells, lasers and data storage devices.

Sources indicate that "Biology and electronics are different domains," remarked Kavya S. Keremane, co-corresponding author and postdoctoral researcher in materials science and engineering at Penn State. "Bridging these two fields required developing an entirely upcoming materials platform that allows them to function seamlessly together. By combining the information storage capabilities of DNA with the exceptional electronic properties of perovskite semiconductors, we created a bio-hybrid system that fundamentally changes how low-power memory devices can be designed.".

Building a Low Power Memory Device.

Sources indicate that using these materials, the team created a memory resistor, known as a "memristor," that operates with very little energy. Unlike ordinary resistors, which maintain a set resistance to electrical current in devices ranging from cell phones to space shuttles and lose their stored information when power disappears, memristors can preserve a record of previous electrical activity. They can remember the direction in which current previously flowed even after the power source is removed.

It has been revealed that that ability allows information to be stored and processed in the same place, resembling the way neurons function in the brain. Such an arrangement could support more simultaneous and sophisticated forms of data processing. According to the researchers, however, practical commercial systems would still require enough storage capacity and electrical power to become costly and inefficient without DNA's ability to pack enormous amounts of information into a very small space while consuming little energy.

"As the demand for artificial intelligence (AI) grows, we need a newly introduced strategy for low-power, high-storage devices," said Bed Poudel, co-corresponding author and research professor of materials science and engineering at Penn State.

Poudel said AI and other emerging technologies are expected to depend increasingly on neuromorphic computing, which is designed to operate more like the human brain. Such systems can evaluate multiple inputs at once while making decisions informed by previous experiences and future priorities.

Industry observers note that "Usually, it takes more power to store more information. Our device, however, consumes 100 times less power and the storage capacity is higher than traditional storage devices, like flash drives.".

Engineering DNA to Conduct Electricity.

To construct the device, the researchers added silver nanoparticles to a layer of customized DNA sequences -- specially designed to be of certain compositions and lengths -- that was integrated with thin films of perovskite.

Sources indicate that this technique, called "doping," involves introducing a small amount of another material to produce specific properties. In this case, adding the silver nanoparticles allowed the DNA to conduct electricity while also helping its molecular units line up in a more orderly arrangement.

According to recent reports, synthetic DNA offered another notable advantage over natural DNA. Unlike natural DNA -- long, entangled strands that behave like wet spaghetti when handled -- short and rigid pieces of synthetic DNA can be arranged with much greater precision at extremely small scales.

In a recent development, according to co-author Neela H. Yennawar, research professor and director of the Penn State Huck Institutes of the Life Sciences' Biomolecular Interactions Core Facility, molecularly engineered DNA can provide structural organization, adjustable electrical conductivity and functional control that natural DNA cannot achieve when incorporated into thin films.

Sources indicate that "We can computationally determine exactly which sequences we need and how long they should be, and then we can rationally design them with synthetic DNA," Yennawar said. "These structures can be systematically doped with silver and other ions and engineered to interface seamlessly with perovskites -- transforming DNA from a biological macromolecule into a programmable, multifunctional nanomaterials platform.".

DNA and Perovskite Work Better Together.

When combined, the silver-doped DNA and perovskite formed bio-hybrid pathways that directed the flow of electrical current through the device.

It has been revealed that the researchers found that electrons moved reliably when they applied less than 0.1 volt -- for comparison, standard U.S. outlets have 120 volts -- and the device responded predictably when the direction of the current was changed.

Industry observers note that the carefully designed DNA structures, combined with the perovskite, also helped make the device unusually stable. According to the team, it continued operating consistently at temperatures approaching 250 degrees Fahrenheit and remained functional at room temperature for more than six weeks, substantially exceeding the performance standards of existing perovskite-based memory storage devices.

According to recent reports, the researchers also reported that the latest system could perform the same memory function as comparable technologies while consuming only one-tenth as much power. That level of efficiency could make the approach especially attractive for future electronics designed to handle large amounts of information with lower energy demands.

"Using just the DNA or just perovskite alone did not produce near as robust a result as the combination," Keremane said. "It's this combination that enables a very high memory storage density that requires very little power.".

A New Direction for Bio-Inspired Electronics.

The team now intends to improve the technology further and explore additional uses for bio-inspired electronic systems.

"Nature has the solution -- we just have to find it and apply it," Poudel mentioned. "This work of integrating DNA into electronics to do amazing things gives a glimpse into what is possible.".

In addition to Keremane, Yennawar and Poudel, other Penn State co-authors include co-corresponding author Luyao Zheng, postdoctoral research in materials science and engineering; Haodong Wu, doctoral student in materials science and engineering; Jiamao Zheng, who was a master's student in materials science and engineering at the time of research and has since graduated from Penn State; Shashank Priya, who was a professor of materials science and engineering at the time of research; and Chiranth C. Ravi, who was a master's student in the Huck Institutes of the Life Sciences at the time of research and has since graduated from Penn State. Abhinav Gorthy and co-corresponding author Rashmi Jha, chemical engineering and materials science, University of Minnesota, also contributed.

The U.S. National Science Foundation, the National Institutes of Health, Penn State and the University of Minnesota supported this research.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Twitch star Ibai Llanos left a small GTA 6 streamer in tears after encouraging his followers to tune into his broadcast, which had no viewers.

The launch of GTA 6 on November 19 saw countless content creators flock to Twitch to stream Rockstar’s long-awaited game, with some of the platform’s biggest personalities attracting enormous audiences.

However, Spanish streaming sensation Ibai Llanos decided to turn his attention to the other end of the spectrum, searching for a GTA 6 streamer with no viewers in the hopes of giving them a boost.

As reported by Meristation, Ibai discovered a Dominican streamer named Dicrim_RD69, who was broadcasting his playthrough of GTA 6 to an audience of zero people.

After joining the broadcast himself, Ibai left a simple “Hello” in the chat before encouraging his followers on social media to visit the channel, follow the streamer, and keep him organization.

His strategy worked, with Dicrim’s audience skyrocketing to 3,243 concurrent viewers within hours. Initially laughing in disbelief at his sudden popularity, Dicrim became overwhelmed with emotion after discovering Ibai was responsible.

It has been revealed that “Thank you. You guys have brought me to tears,” he said. “Ibai, I love you. I’ve been a fan of Ibai for a long time.”.

The pair subsequently spoke over a video call, during which Dicrim revealed that he had been streaming for more than a year without attracting much of an audience.

“When you don’t have someone to talk to, to communicate with, you don’t feel the same. You feel bad,” he explained, admitting he had been feeling particularly upset the previous night.

Ibai reassured him by recalling his own beginnings as a content creator, revealing that he and his cousin used to stream basketball commentary to zero viewers when he was just 14 years old.

“If it makes you happy, keep doing it,” Ibai encouraged him. Dicrim, who explained that his family couldn’t afford video games when he was younger, thanked Ibai for the gesture. “You made me the happiest man in the world,” he remarked.

#126560. Vice City was the GTA that established Rockstar's killer formula - and 24 years on, it's still one of the best games ever made

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2096 w)

Vice City was the GTA that established Rockstar's killer formula - and 24 years on, it's still one of the best games ever made

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2096 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • "Get the limey out of here," Burt Reynolds tells the producers of GTA: Vice City during a recording session for the game, as Rockstar co-founder Dan Houser enters the studio.
  • Recent findings suggest that I can't verify the truth of this story.
  • Industry observers note that and I'm not saying that in a pejorative way at all.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"Get the limey out of here," Burt Reynolds tells the producers of GTA: Vice City during a recording session for the game, as Rockstar co-founder Dan Houser enters the studio. "I'm not going to work if this limey Brit is in here!" Houser refuses to leave, so the story goes - he just came down to meet one of his heroes! - and he and Reynolds end up chest-to-chest, about to come to blows, before a studio engineer breaks up the fight.

Recent findings suggest that I can't verify the truth of this story. It's one of those development rumours that's been around for a long time, originally written in a book about how games conquered pop culture called "All Your Base Are Belong to Us" by Harold Goldberg. But I like to believe it's true, because in this one moment, the two crucial strands of GTA: Vice City's DNA helix together: its star power and Rockstar's arrogance.

Industry observers note that and I'm not saying that in a pejorative way at all. I think a game of Vice City's scope - stretched to breaking with ambition, budget, and technical wizardry - couldn't exist without the ego trip of Rockstar at its highest. This is a game that (somehow!) started as a bit of DLC for GTA 3, supposedly intended to launch as a mission pack when Rockstar North figured out how to port it to PC. GTA 3 rolled out in October 2001, and by some miracle - and lots of crunch, no doubt - Vice City hit shelves in October 2002.

This game - a game that would come to represent everything the GTA series is, for generations to come - was put together in about a year. I'd feel pretty full of myself, too, if I was able to crank out that sort of quality in that sort of timeframe. With a development budget of approximately $5 million (massive at the time, even though it seems paltry against GTA 6's rumoured $1 billion+) and a marketing spend of $13.2 million, Vice City's budget was indicative of a series shifting toward becoming a cultural milestone - a standard bearer for video games as a whole, and as explosive and attention-grabbing as Hollywood's biggest events.

It's not like Rockstar needed to borrow credibility from the movie industry to inject some panache into its work, but even so, I think it's in its vortex of unbelievable Hollywood talent that Vice City really makes its mark. This was the first time Rockstar used a voiced protagonist, and by the developer's own admission, it was "a riddle" they had to solve. It didn't come easy; by making the protagonist a fullyfleshed-out character, players also had to like him - not an easy ask when he's a bonafide psychopath with a fetish for revenge like Tommy Vercetti. But Ray Liotta pulls it off without breaking a sweat. The actor has gone on record saying it was a rough gig ("You're creating a character that's not there before", he bizarrely complained in one interview), and Vice City director Navid Khonsari often moaned about the actor's unpredictable moods, so I imagine the mood in the booth wasn't great, but the result? The result is phenomenal.

You shouldn't like Vercetti. He's arrogant, he's brash, he's a totem for all the worst elements of misogynistic 80s excess. And yet, because he's such a cartoon caricature of a Miami gangster, he becomes a sort of quasi-romantic figure; a mob stooge who's been set up by his old 'business associates' and by the very fabric of the American Dream. Vice City is, in a sense, a redemption story dressed in the clothes of a revenge one. Vercetti dreams of being a self-made man, of taming this new frontier of unbridled capitalism and clawing back the years that were taken from him by the mob in Liberty City.

Sources indicate that from the moment he arrives in town and a cocaine deal rapidly goes south, Vercetti is on the back foot. In the opening hours of the game, he - and, of course, you by extension - work for pocket change, picking up menial jobs here and there while meeting all the freaks and strangers Vice City has to offer. There are no less than 50 story characters here, brought to life by Ray Liotta, Tom Sizemore, Luis Guzmán, Gary Busey, Danny Trejo, Debbie Harry, Danny Dyer, Philip Michael Thomas, William Fichtner, and many, many more besides.

Recent findings suggest that playing Vice City again in 2026, I was absolutely floored by this cast - and how well their personalities and mannerisms translate to the almost puppet-like visuals Rockstar deployed for the game. Reynolds - despite not having a good time in the booth, if the story up top is anything to go by - is a highlight; the bombast and bravado of his Avery Carrington feels like a prototype for some of the more extreme characters we meet later in the series. I think I can even see a bit of Trevor in him, you know? It's how the Housers would take a trope - say, ruthless Texan oil magnate - and amplify it to its furthest, most cartoon extreme: what does this person look like with all the guardrails off, with the heady intoxication of unlimited capital at their disposal? For Trevor, that trope is 'unhinged redneck' and the cartoonish extreme is 'without a single shred of a conscience'. You can apply the formula to just about anything in the series, and it makes sense.

Industry observers note that for Tommy Vercetti, though, it's slightly more nuanced. He isn't just 'Scarface' with a touch more humanity - no, he's a tragic figure, betrayed by all his closest friends. In striving to take back some power and gain a little more control over his life, he ends up decapitating the local drug smuggling scene and taking over as its head. The first half of Vice City is Sisyphean; an endless, uphill slog to scrabble just enough money to get by. Then, all of a sudden, the world opens up: you're now head of a drug smuggling ring, operating out of a suspiciously Scarface-like mansion, with the city at your fingertips.

It has been revealed that the way the game, previously tightly-coiled and a bit miserly with its freedom, now unfurls in front of you is a perfect reflection of this upcoming-found power. Suddenly, your world isn't governed by the little mission icons on your minimap, you're not being told what to do over the phone by contacts wanting something from you. No, you're calling the shots. This is the 80s, so those that are making it big are making it big, and those that are failing are failing. In a breathless display of uber-capitalist Yuppie thinking, you can even buy out nearly-bankrupt businesses and run them to your liking. The strategy is two-fold: one, you gain fronts for your other illicit activities, and two, you diversify your income streams and safeguard your assets should any one element fail.

According to recent reports, and it's here, in its glorious second half, that Vice City becomes a breezy, beautiful bit of open-world catnip that fuses gameplay and story in a way few games have done so successfully since. You can buy a strip club (where you can launder cash), the Malibu Club (which comes with an outlandish set of missions culminating in a heist), the Cherry Popper ice cream van manufacturer (a front for dealing), the boatyard (a drug smuggling base run by two excellent potheads), Sunshine Autos (a fence for stolen cars), Kaufman Cabs (headed up by an old controller played by Debbie Harry), Interglobal Studios (an adult movie production company), and the Print Works (a counterfeiting operation). The roleplaying as Vercetti takes off; you're a bigshot touring his empire, helping out here and there, meeting your crew, setting up deals. This should feel like drudgery; workaday tedium unbecoming for a legitimate businessman like yourself. But every job, every bit of flavour text and dialogue, feeds into your growing sense of power… and Vercetti's unstoppable ego.

Alongside these key story beats are Vice City's non-essential tasks - which feel like a precursor to the 'Strangers and Freaks' missions in later GTA and Red Dead games - including the Love Fist missions. These, I think, are the best missions in the game (I'd also like to note here that 'Jez Torrent' is an amazing name for a Latest Wave of British Heavy metal frontman). But it's the way these core and non-essential missions dovetail that feels so great, and where the open world of Vice City really comes into its own.

In many ways, Rockstar's work here created the blueprint for what would become the Grand Theft Auto 'formula'; galvanising cinematic setpieces with free-roam activities and meta-progression that manage to alloy player agency with this sense of perpetual, unstoppable momentum. And it's all fun, too. There are some abysmal tasks, sure - piloting RC aircraft to ruin building sites, navigating boats with the wonkiest physics you've ever seen around stunt courses, waiting 15 minutes a pop for rare cars to spawn - but generally speaking, Vice City has the fun factor.

I don't think that's something I can say of other GTA games: I think often, they're a bit bloated around the middle, padded out with baggy missions and feckless busywork to give the illusion of depth and breadth. GTA 4 is also one of the most dour and oppressive open worlds I've experienced (this is a compliment, mostly), but it's not particularly fun. GTA 5, especially the Trevor segments out in the rural counties, can get a bit one-note - why introduce us to this massive world, to the state of Los Santos, if you're going to quarantine us to the rural outskirts when we're just starting to familiarise ourselves with the city? Why put up rails in a world begging us to revel in its open-ended sandbox? The only time that happens in Vice City is at the start, and the game is better for it: 'if you want to live the Scarface fantasy, buddy, you've got to earn it'.

Sources indicate that and there's so much to love about the vibes of Vice City. The guys in shorts smoking pot on the beach; the girls in bikinis rollerblading down the promenade; the neon-drenched slick of a Florida night in the rain; the still-unbelievable who's who of music, deployed with panache in certain cutscenes; the incidental chatter of coked-up presenters on the radio; the distinct realisation of the Haitian and Cuban districts on the map; how 'downtown' actually feels like downtown. You'd think all this would have aged out of relevance by now - especially with GTA 5 being as lush and premium as it is - so it's a real credit to all those Rockstar employees that no doubt spent countless nights sleeping under their desks that Vice City still feels this good now, in 2026.

GTA: Vice City is still one of the best games ever made, I think, and probably one of the most important, too. Buoyed by Rockstar's ambition, and propelled to mainstream success by the strength of its cast, it represented video games coming out of their awkward teenage years and blossoming into young adults; biting off slightly more than they could chew, but cocksure and confident all at the same time.

Industry observers note that given how much of Vice City is built around the visibility and power of its cast, it's disappointing we're never going to see these characters really represented in any other GTA title again. Liotta, already unhappy about the process of recording his lines, reportedly refused to come back as Vercetti for San Andreas. And that's a real shame because - by former lead writer Dan Houser's own admission - Liotta saved his "awful writing" with his talent. The actor passed away in May 2022.

It has been revealed that though he balked with Reynolds, Vice City director Khonsari could usually corral the rampant ego of his Hollywood hires in the GTA studio. "If you want me to break it down to you," he’d say, "these games gross over half a billion dollars, more than all of your movies put together!" I think you can see that bravado in the spirit of Vice City, and reflected in the runaway ego of Tommy Vercetti. And I think - without that almost toxic sense of self-belief - Vice City would never have happened.

Latest Update: NASA just used satellites and debris to navigate without GPS

📅 26 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (779 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • NASA's Starling mission has reached another milestone in autonomous spaceflight by demonstrating a system that can determine a satellite's orbital position using other objects in space as reference points rather than depending on an external navigation network.
  • Industry observers note that the technology, called FALCON (Fast Autonomous Lost-in-space Catalog-based Optical Navigation), is designed to help spacecraft operate with greater independence.
  • Satellites near Earth commonly rely on GPS for navigation, but those signals may be weak, unreliable, or unavailable around the Moon and in deep space.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NASA's Starling mission has reached another milestone in autonomous spaceflight by demonstrating a system that can determine a satellite's orbital position using other objects in space as reference points rather than depending on an external navigation network.

Industry observers note that the technology, called FALCON (Fast Autonomous Lost-in-space Catalog-based Optical Navigation), is designed to help spacecraft operate with greater independence. Such capabilities could become increasingly key as NASA pursues missions farther from Earth, including lunar satellite swarms, distributed science missions, and future human exploration.

Satellites near Earth commonly rely on GPS for navigation, but those signals may be weak, unreliable, or unavailable around the Moon and in deep space. FALCON offers an alternative by allowing spacecraft to determine where they are using what they can observe around them.

Industry observers note that the FALCON payload is a joint flight experiment developed by NASA and EraDrive, a startup that emerged from Stanford University. The system combines EraDrive's Era-Core flight software and embedded algorithms with Starling's cameras and an onboard catalog of known satellites. Together, these tools enable GPS-independent navigation while also helping the spacecraft track activity and objects in its surroundings.

According to recent reports, "FALCON is yet another success for the Starling demonstration mission. The results from FALCON can have far-reaching implications for on-orbit space-traffic monitoring, collision avoidance, and alternative navigation," stated Roger Hunter, program manager for NASA's Small Spacecraft and Distributed Systems program at NASA's Ames Research Center in California's Silicon Valley. "The number of 'firsts' from Starling just keeps growing.".

Using Satellites and Debris as Reference Points.

The FALCON demonstration evaluated two related capabilities using Starling's onboard star tracker cameras. These cameras are standard spacecraft instruments that detect bright objects in space and help determine a spacecraft's orientation and position.

According to recent reports, during position, navigation, and timing experiments, FALCON identified objects seen by Starling's cameras, including other spacecraft and orbital debris, and compared them with a publicly available catalog of known space objects maintained by the U.S. Department of War. Once the observed objects were identified and verified, FALCON used them as reference points to calculate Starling's orbit.

Recent findings suggest that A separate set of experiments tested whether the spacecraft could improve orbital estimates for the objects it observed. Mission controllers loaded a catalog containing approximately 20,000 space objects and their predicted orbits onto Starling.

Over a period of three days, FALCON improved the known orbits of more than 200 objects without any intervention from operators on the ground.

A First for Autonomous Optical Navigation.

According to recent reports, FALCON's ability to determine its own orbit represents a first for a spacecraft navigating with optical cameras based on its position relative to other objects in space. In separate catalog updating tests, Starling also generated better onboard predictions of object positions than those supplied by ground stations.

These abilities could be especially valuable for future networks of satellites operating without GPS. Coordinated satellite systems may play an crucial role in supporting human activities on the surfaces of the Moon or Mars.

Sources indicate that precise spacecraft positioning is also essential for distributed science missions, where measurements collected from several locations in space must be accurately aligned. For space traffic management, autonomous navigation and onboard catalog updates could reduce dependence on ground-based tracking networks while improving collision avoidance.

From University Research to Commercial Technology.

The FALCON experiment also demonstrates NASA's role in helping university research develop into commercial technology. The work began as a University SmallSat Technology Partnerships project before developing into EraDrive, which is now commercializing its Era-Core software and related hardware for wider use.

Starling gave the technology an opportunity to be tested under real conditions in orbit, demonstrating how advanced flight software can allow satellites to function as increasingly autonomous navigators.

It has been revealed that later this year, Starling, which launched in 2023, will expand the FALCON experiment using Era-Core. The mission's four spacecraft will share tracking information with one another and use those combined observations to refine their positions collectively.

NASA's Ames Research Center in California's Silicon Valley leads the Starling mission. NASA's Small Spacecraft and Distributed Systems program, based at Ames and within the Research and Technology Mission Directorate, funds and manages the Starling mission.

An Indian YouTuber accused of stealing $1.8 million worth of jewellery has been forced to reenact the alleged heist for police after a distinctive tattoo helped investigators identify him.

On November 12, approximately 11.4kg of gold and diamond jewellery worth roughly 150,000,000 Indian rupees ($1.6 million) was discovered missing from a newly opened Tanishq jewellery showroom in Madurai, India.

Police believe the thief entered the building overnight using scaffolding at an adjacent construction site before descending through an unfinished elevator shaft and escaping with bags of valuables.

According to India Today, CCTV footage indicated that the suspect had visited the store three times before the robbery, apparently to familiarize himself with its layout.

Despite wearing a mask, a distinctive tattoo visible in the footage reportedly helped investigators identify him as 25-year-old YouTuber Nishanth Krishna.

Sources indicate that days later, Nishanth was arrested after a bus driver recognized him and alerted police. According to The Latest Indian Express, he allegedly attempted to escape through a bus window as officers approached.

His girlfriend, fellow content creator Meenakshi Nachiyar and his father were also arrested in connection with the heist, with police alleging they helped conceal the stolen jewellery.

On November 20, Nishanth was taken back to the showroom and instructed to reenact the robbery, demonstrating how he entered the building, collected the jewellery, and escaped.

As reported by Hindustan Times, he was subsequently returned to Madurai Central Prison and remanded in judicial custody.

Breaking: What's the best GTA?
