Sending a document for signature is the easy part of an e-signature integration. One POST request and the signer gets an email. The work that actually breaks in production happens afterwards: knowing when the document was signed, trusting the notification that told you so, handling the same notification twice, and getting the final PDF into storage before the download link expires.

This tutorial builds that whole loop in Node.js with Express. An event in your app (a deal is approved, a client is onboarded, a task moves to "ready to sign") sends a contract from a template. When the signer finishes, a webhook arrives, your server verifies it, and the signed PDF plus its audit trail get saved without anyone touching them.

It has been revealed that the code uses Firma.dev, the e-signature API I work on, because I needed a real API to make the examples runnable. The patterns are not specific to it, though. Signature verification, idempotent handlers, short-lived download URLs, and reconciliation jobs show up in almost every webhook-driven integration, and the same structure applies whether you're receiving events from a payment processor, a CI system, or another signing provider.

Sources indicate that there's a fifth part that tutorials usually skip: a reconciliation job that catches anything the webhooks missed. We'll build that too, because webhooks are a notification mechanism, not a delivery guarantee.

Set three environment variables:.

It has been revealed that before sending anything, wrap the HTTP calls in one place. This is where authentication lives, and it's also where you handle 429 Too Many Requests once instead of in every caller. Most APIs, this one included, return a Retry-After header on a 429, so the client should honour it rather than guessing a backoff.

The 503 branch matters later. When a document has just been completed, the final PDF and its completion certificate take a moment to generate, and the download endpoint says so with a 503 and a Retry-After instead of handing you a half-built file.

The trigger depends on your product. It might be a route handler, a queue consumer, or a CRM automation calling into your service. What matters is that the function doing the sending is small and takes plain data:.

Two design choices are worth calling out.

It has been revealed that use a single create-and-send call when you can. Many signing APIs split this into "create a draft" and "send the draft." That's useful when a human needs to review the document first, but for automation it creates a window where your process can crash between the two calls and leave an orphaned draft. A combined endpoint makes the operation atomic from your side.

Store the provider's ID on your own record immediately. Webhook payloads reference the signing request, not your deal or customer. Without that mapping you'll end up searching by email address, which falls apart as soon as one client signs two documents.

Here's the first place integrations quietly go wrong. Webhook signatures are computed over the exact bytes the sender transmitted. If Express parses the body as JSON first, you lose those bytes, and re-serialising the object won't reproduce them (key order, whitespace, and number formatting can all change). Signature checks then fail intermittently, which is the worst kind of failure.

The fix is to use express.raw() on the webhook route only, so the handler receives a Buffer:.

Recent findings suggest that most webhook providers sign payloads with HMAC-SHA256 using a shared secret. The details vary, so read your provider's docs for the exact header format, but the scheme here is common: the header looks like t=1731456000,v1=5f2b..., and the signed string is the timestamp, a dot, and the raw body. Stripe uses a very similar format, and the Standard Webhooks spec describes the same idea as a vendor-neutral convention.

Each line here defends against something specific.

The OWASP guidance on cryptographic storage covers the other half of this: the secret belongs in an environment variable or secrets manager, never in the repository.

Every serious webhook system delivers at least once, not exactly once. If your endpoint is slow, returns a 5xx, or the network drops the response, the sender retries. Firma.dev, for example, makes up to three attempts per event (immediately, then after at least five minutes, then after at least an hour) and treats anything other than a 2xx as a failure, including redirects. Other providers retry more aggressively. Either way, your handler will eventually see the same event twice.

According to recent reports, the defence is to record each event's unique ID and skip ones you've seen. In the server above that's alreadyProcessed and markProcessed. For a demo, a Set works:.

In production, use your database and let a unique constraint do the work, so two concurrent deliveries can't both pass the check:.

Also notice the order in the route: respond with 200, then do the work. Many providers time out deliveries after a few seconds (five, in this case). Downloading a PDF and uploading it to object storage can easily take longer than that, and a timeout counts as a failure, which triggers a retry, which triggers duplicate work. Acknowledging fast and processing asynchronously avoids that loop.

According to recent reports, setImmediate is fine for a tutorial, but it has a real weakness: if the process dies after sending the 200 and before finishing the work, the event is acknowledged and lost. In production, push the event onto a durable queue (BullMQ, SQS, a jobs table) before responding. Step 7 covers the safety net for whatever still slips through.

Now the actual business logic. You'll usually see several event types (sent, viewed, a signer signed, declined, expired, completed). Only one of them means "the document is final":.

Three things in here are easy to get wrong.

Sources indicate that don't treat "a signer signed" as "the document is done." With multiple signers, each one triggers its own event, and a per-signer "all complete" flag can be true on more than one of them. Key your storage logic off the single completion event.

It has been revealed that don't persist the download URL. Pre-signed URLs expire (this one carries an expires_at). Saving the link to your database and serving it to users later produces broken links a few minutes or hours later. Download the bytes and store them in storage you control. Swapping the fs.writeFile calls for an S3 PutObject or a Google Drive upload is a drop-in change.

Sources indicate that store the audit trail, not just the PDF. If a signature is ever disputed, the PDF reveals what was signed, and the audit trail shows who signed it, when, and from where (timestamps, IP addresses, the sequence of views and signatures). That evidence is what makes an electronic signature defensible, which brings us to the legal side.

Retries are finite. Endpoints go down during deploys. Some providers auto-disable a webhook after enough consecutive failures, and events aren't guaranteed to arrive in order. Any one of these can leave a completed document sitting unsaved.

A small scheduled job closes that gap. Keep a list of signing requests your app considers "pending," and periodically ask the API for their real status:.

Industry observers note that since storeSignedDocument overwrites by ID, running it twice for the same document is harmless. That's the property you want from every step in a webhook pipeline: doing it again shouldn't change the result.

None of this is legal advice, but a few facts shape how you build.

It has been revealed that in the US, the ESIGN Act and the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act (adopted by 49 states) give electronic signatures the same legal standing as handwritten ones for most commercial documents. ESIGN also has requirements around consumer consent and record retention, which is part of why you store the final PDF yourself rather than relying on a third-party link.

Recent findings suggest that in the EU, eIDAS defines three levels: simple (SES), advanced (AdES), and qualified (QES). SES and AdES cover most business contracts. QES requires a qualified trust service provider and certificate-based identity, and some documents (certain property transfers and court filings, depending on the country) require it or exclude e-signatures entirely. Check which level your document types need before you pick a provider, since not every API offers every level.

Industry observers note that across jurisdictions, the evidence that holds up is the same: who signed, how they were identified, when it happened, and proof the document hasn't changed since. That's the audit trail and the completion certificate, which is why Step 6 stores both.

If you're evaluating providers for a workflow like this, the questions that matter at the integration level are mostly not on the pricing page:.

Recent findings suggest that the send call is one line. The reliability comes from everything around it: keeping the raw body for verification, checking timestamps and comparing in constant time, acknowledging fast and deduplicating by event ID, downloading files before their links expire, and running a reconciliation job for the events that never arrive. Get those right and contract signing becomes something your app does in the background, with no one chasing signatures or copying PDFs between folders.

Abernathy is an unlikely hero forced into leadership in the rebellion by circumstances out of his control. This doesn’t mean the C-suite can’t learn a thing or two from him. Here are a few quick stats on the franchise and some of Haymitch’s best management lessons. [Image: Lionsgate] The Hunger Games franchise by the numbers The Hunger Games by Suzanne Collins, the first book in the original trilogy, was published by Scholastic on September 14, 2008. It was followed by Catching Fire in 2009 and Mockingjay in 2010. Before the second book even came out, Lionsgate acquired the film rights for the first book. It was a smart move because the four Hunger Games films have collectively made more than $1.45 billion at the domestic box office. Collins took a break after the first trilogy. A stand-alone prequel novel, The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes, came out in 2020, telling the backstory of Coriolanus Snow. The 2023 film version made more than $166 million at the domestic box office. Sunrise on the Reaping was published in 2025. According to Deadline, the new film is expected to make at least $80 million at the domestic box office on opening weekend alone. Haymitch Abernathy: Reluctant leader archetype Haymitch Abernathy, played by Woody Harrelson in the original films and Joseph Zada in Sunrise, is an unconventional leader. He would rather be drinking away his sorrows than changing the fate of Panem—but sometimes management is thrust upon us. Abernathy excels at strategic planning. In the original books and movies, he is able to guide Peeta and Katniss through the games two times while organizing a rebellion right under the Capitol’s nose. This comes through very careful planning and deception. In the real world, however, business leaders need to be able to communicate a clear vision and how to execute it. Abernathy is rough around the edges—and his tough exterior allows him to work with a diverse range of difficult colleagues to get results. You could call him a people-first strategist. For instance, he was able to get through to Katniss and help her play the public relations game by pretending to have feelings for Peeta. She did that so well that her love for him ended up becoming real. In addition, Abernathy got the vain people of the Capitol to empathize with Katniss and Peeta and send them lifesaving supplies like medicine and water. Plan, collaborate, and adapt Similarly, managers will have to work with many different personalities, departments, or vendors. True leaders can approach each individual or organization in a way that uplifts their strengths. Back in Panem, all this planning doesn’t mean the reluctant Abernathy can’t adapt. He thrives under pressure. He was the victor of the 50th Hunger Games, the Second Quarter Quell. He had to compete against 47 other tributes, double the usual amount. He won by using the force field around the arena against his opponent. In business, as in the Hunger Games, not everything is going to go according to the five-year-plan. Sometimes you have to improvise solutions as problems arise. As it hits theaters, Sunrise will reveal more of Abernathy’s story and administrative prowess. The business world should take note.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Qwen3-8B is one of the most exciting recent releases—a model with native agentic capabilities, making it a natural fit for the AIPC.
  • With OpenVINO.GenAI, we’ve been able to accelerate generation by ~1.3× using speculative decoding with a lightweight Qwen3-0.6B draft.
  • By using speculative decoding and applying a simple pruning process to the draft, we pushed the speedup even further to ~1.4×.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Qwen3-8B is one of the most exciting recent releases—a model with native agentic capabilities, making it a natural fit for the AIPC.

With OpenVINO.GenAI, we’ve been able to accelerate generation by ~1.3× using speculative decoding with a lightweight Qwen3-0.6B draft.

By using speculative decoding and applying a simple pruning process to the draft, we pushed the speedup even further to ~1.4×.

We wrapped this up by showing how these improvements can be used to run a fast, local AI Agent with 🤗 smolagents.

According to recent reports, qwen3-8B is part of the latest Qwen family, trained with explicit agentic behaviors. It supports tool invocation, multi-step reasoning, and long-context handling capabilities, that make it well-suited for complex agent workflows. When integrated with frameworks like Hugging Face 🤗smolagents, QwenAgent, or AutoGen, it enables a wide range of agentic applications built around tool use and reasoning. Unlike single-turn chatbots, agentic applications rely on reasoning models that produce “thinking aloud” traces, intermediate steps that expand token usage, making inference speed critical to responsiveness. The combination of optimized inference and built-in agentic intelligence makes Qwen3-8B a compelling foundation for next-gen AI agents.

We started by benchmarking the 4-bit optimized OpenVINO version of Qwen3-8B on an Intel Lunar Lake integrated GPU, establishing this as our baseline for further acceleration.

It has been revealed that speculative decoding is a method to speed up auto-regressive generation. It works by using a smaller, faster model as a draft to propose multiple tokens in a single forward pass, which are then validated by the larger target model in one forward pass. In our setup, Qwen3-8B served as the target model while Qwen3-0.6B was used as the draft. This approach delivered an average of 1.3× speedup over the baseline.

It has been revealed that before initializing the LLMPipeline, make sure both the target and draft models are converted to OpenVINO. You can either download pre-converted models from the provided links or follow these instructions to convert your own.

Industry observers note that the speculative decoding speedup depends on the average number of generated tokens per forward step of the target, γ \gamma γ, the speculation window size, and the ratio between the target and draft models' latency c c c. A smaller, faster (though less accurate) draft can often deliver greater acceleration. This inspired us to shrink the draft model while still preserving its quality, i.e. E(#generated_tokens) E(\# generated\_tokens) E(#generated_tokens).

Speedup=E(#generated_tokens)γc+1 Speedup = \frac{E(\# generated\_tokens)}{\gamma c + 1} Speedup=γc+1E(#generated_tokens)​.

Recent findings suggest that our recent work reveals that model depth (number of layers) is a major contributor to inference latency. We drew inspiration from recent work on layer-wise compression[1]. In our approach, we identify blocks of layers that contribute little, measured using angular distance, and remove them. After pruning, we apply fine-tuning to recover accuracy. Using this method, we pruned 6 out of 28 layers from the Qwen3-0.6B draft model. To recover the quality of the pruned draft model, we further finetuned it using synthetic data generated by Qwen3-8B. The data was produced by generating responses to 500k prompts from BAAI/Infinity-Instruct dataset.

According to recent reports, the resulting pruned draft model delivered ~1.4x speedup compared to the baseline, an improvement over the ~1.3× gain achieved with the original draft. This outcome aligns with theoretical expectations - reducing draft latency improves the over-all speedup, enabling faster and more efficient inference.

This demonstrates how pruning + speculative decoding can unlock faster and more efficient inference—making local AI agents even more practical.

Check out the notebook and the Qwen3-0.6B depth-pruned draft model to reproduce our results step by step.

Sources indicate that to showcase the real-world potential, we deployed our optimized setup with the 🤗smolagents library. With this integration, developers can plug in Qwen3-8B (paired with our pruned draft) to build agents that call APIs and external tools, write and execute code, handle long-context reasoning and run efficiently on Intel® Core™ Ultra. The benefits aren’t limited to Hugging Face, this model pairing can also be used seamlessly with frameworks like AutoGen or QwenAgent, further strengthening the agentic ecosystem.

In our demo, we assigned the accelerated Qwen3-based agent a task: 👉 Summarize the key features of the Qwen3 model series and present them in a slide deck.

Here’s how it worked: 1. The agent used a web search tool to gather up-to-date information. 2. It then switched to the Python interpreter to generate slides with the python-pptx library. This simple workflow highlights just a fraction of the possibilities unlocked when accelerated Qwen3 models meet frameworks like 🤗smolagents, bringing practical, efficient AI agents to life on AI PC. ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that early this year, we let every employee at ClickUp build their own AI agents and skills.
  • When we looked into which AIs brought the most value, there was an obvious pattern.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Early this year, we let every employee at ClickUp build their own AI agents and skills. Within months, we were running five agents for every employee, which felt like a transformation until we looked at the actual output and efficiency. In my own finance org, only 30% of employee-built agents and skills actually moved the needle. When we looked into which AIs brought the most value, there was an obvious pattern. The successful agents were created by employees who understood where a process in their work typically tends to break, and could turn that knowledge into clear rules and processes for artificial intelligence. We went from treating AI skill-building as an open invitation and instead focused on the people who were building AI agents that moved the needle. That fixed the quality problem, but handed us a harder problem to solve. When you take your best talent’s craft and turn it into an AI agent, what does that employee get in return for their expertise and labor? As more companies have the best employees train their AI, leaders must have a response to this question. Define the bar, then pay against it When we changed our AI skill-building process, eligibility depended on a manager’s recommendation and a strong performance review. But identifying the right people is half the work. Companies also need to establish what qualifies as a high-value skill, and what it is worth, before anyone starts building one. We created a framework that categorizes skills, assigns value, and determines the reward. It’s simple but makes it clear what employees should aim for and gives us a consistent way to reward them. At ClickUp, every skill falls into one of four categories, and each category has its own measure of success. One, revenue acceleration skills are measured by the pipeline or bookings they add, and two, cost elimination skills are measured by the spend they remove, like canceling a software we no longer use. Time compression skills, three, are measured by how much faster a core process runs, like closing the books or responding to a customer. And executive bounties, four, are specific problems our leadership team has identified, each with a reward attached. The category tells employees what type of skills to build with AI, but the proof of impact is what determines how much the AI skill is worth. Before creating a latest AI skill, employees must record where the measure stands today, like how many sales meetings aren’t rebooked each month or how long it takes to close the books. Then they can build, and once the AI skill has been running long enough to show a consistent pattern of value, finance compares the new numbers against the starting point. Finance then subtracts the cost of running the AI skill, including tools and maintenance, and what remains is the value the employee created. We then look at what we would have paid to get the same result a different way. Hiring even a few experienced sellers is a major expense, so when one person’s AI skills deliver that same capacity, a standard raise no longer reflects what their work is worth to the business. To determine the reward, we also consider how long the value will last. A skill that solves a single, contained problem earns a bonus. A skill or system the employee will keep running and improving earns a permanent raise, since the tech giant will keep benefiting from that work every year. Together, these steps give us a dollar amount for each AI skill created, which we can use to determine the compensation ranging from a one-time bonus to becoming part of our “unicorn” group. Unicorns are employees whose AI work changes what an entire team can do, and they receive a merit increase of more than 30% along with eligibility for compensation up to $1 million at the top of the band. For example, one growth operations manager identified 17 places where we were regularly losing potential sales and built 11 AI skills to address them. Those skills recovered hundreds of thousands of dollars in pipeline and increased the number of sales prospects by 25%. They also saved every sales rep about 90 minutes in their day, which is equivalent to seven sellers’ worth of capacity. Because the results were large, verified, and directly tied to revenue, this employee joined our “unicorn” group. Reward your talent for making their expertise reusable Your best people are already training your AI. They are handing over the part of themselves that made them hard to replace, and the company can keep using that knowledge long after they have moved on. Hoarding what only one person knows feels like job security, but it is ultimately a ceiling. The people thriving in this model build the skill, hand over their knowledge, and move to the next problem. Each handoff allows them to take on a bigger, more interesting challenge. This is the model companies should build toward as AI moves deeper into knowledge work—rewarding people for making their expertise reusable. That judgment is intellectual property, and paying for it is how you build AI that works while retaining top talent.

Latest Update: Introducing RTEB: A Latest Standard for Retrieval Evaluation

📅 01 Oct 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1032 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • TL;DR – We’re excited to introduce the beta version of the Retrieval Embedding Benchmark (RTEB), a fresh benchmark designed to reliably evaluate the retrieval accuracy of embedding models for real-world applications.
  • It has been revealed that the performance of many AI applications, from RAG and agents to recommendation systems, is fundamentally limited by the quality of search and retrieval.
  • The current standard for evaluation often relies on a model's "zero-shot" performance on public benchmarks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TL;DR – We’re excited to introduce the beta version of the Retrieval Embedding Benchmark (RTEB), a fresh benchmark designed to reliably evaluate the retrieval accuracy of embedding models for real-world applications. Existing benchmarks struggle to measure true generalization, while RTEB addresses this with a hybrid strategy of open and private datasets. Its goal is simple: to create a fair, transparent, and application-focused standard for measuring how models perform on data they haven’t seen before.

It has been revealed that the performance of many AI applications, from RAG and agents to recommendation systems, is fundamentally limited by the quality of search and retrieval. As such, accurately measuring the retrieval quality of embedding models is a common pain point for developers. How do you really know how well a model will perform in the wild?

This is where things get tricky. The current standard for evaluation often relies on a model's "zero-shot" performance on public benchmarks. However, this is, at best, an approximation of a model's true generalization capabilities. When models are repeatedly evaluated against the same public datasets, a gap emerges between their reported scores and their actual performance on new, unseen data.

To address these challenges, we developed RTEB, a benchmark built to provide a reliable standard for evaluating retrieval models.

While the underlying evaluation methodology and metrics (such as NDCG@10) are well-known and robust, the integrity of existing benchmarks is often set back by the following issues:.

The Generalization Gap. The current benchmark ecosystem inadvertently encourages "teaching to the test." When training data sources overlap with evaluation datasets, a model's score can become inflated, undermining a benchmark's integrity. This practice, whether intentional or not, is evident in the training datasets of several models. This creates a feedback loop where models are rewarded for memorizing test data rather than developing robust, generalizable capabilities.

Sources indicate that because of the above, models with a lower zero-shot score[1] may perform very well on the benchmark, without generalizing to new problems. For this reason, models with slightly lower benchmark performance and a higher zero-shot score are often recommended instead.

Sources indicate that misalignment with Today’s AI Applications. Many benchmarks are poorly aligned with the enterprise use cases that developers are building today. They often rely on academic datasets or on retrieval tasks derived from QA datasets, which, while useful in their own right, were not designed to evaluate retrieval and can fail to capture the distributional biases and complexities encountered in real-world retrieval scenarios. Benchmarks which do not possess these challenges are often too narrow, focusing on a single domain like code retrieval, making them unsuitable for evaluating general-purpose models.

Recent findings suggest that today, we’re excited to introduce the Retrieval Embedding Benchmark (RTEB). Its goal is to create a latest, reliable, high-quality benchmark that measures the true retrieval accuracy of embedding models.

To combat benchmark overfitting, RTEB implements a hybrid strategy using both open and private datasets:.

It has been revealed that this hybrid approach encourages the development of models with broad, robust generalization. A model with a significant performance drop between the open and the private datasets would suggest overfitting, providing a clear signal to the community. This is already apparent with some models, which show a notable drop in performance on RTEB's private datasets.

RTEB is designed with a particular emphasis on enterprise use cases. Instead of a complex hierarchy, it uses simple groups for clarity. A single dataset can belong to multiple groups (e.g., a German law dataset exists in both the "law" and "German" groups).

In a recent development, A complete list of the datasets can be found below. We strategy to continually patch both the open as well as closed portion with different categories of datasets and actively encourage participation from the community; please open an issue on the MTEB repository on GitHub if you would like to suggest other datasets.

Recent findings suggest that RTEB is launching today in beta. We believe building a robust benchmark is a community effort, and we plan to evolve RTEB based on feedback from developers and researchers alike. We encourage you to share your thoughts, suggest newly introduced datasets, find issues in existing datasets and help us build a more reliable standard for everyone. Please feel free to join the discussion or open an glitch in the MTEB repository on Github.

To highlight areas for improvement we want to be transparent about RTEB's current limitations and our prepares for the future.

Our goal is for RTEB to become a community-trusted standard for retrieval evaluation.

Industry observers note that the RTEB leaderboard is available today on Hugging Face as a part of the new Retrieval section on the MTEB leaderboard. We invite you to check it out, evaluate your models, and join us in building a better, more reliable benchmark for the entire AI community.

In a recent development, [1] Zero-shot score is the proportion of the evaluation set which the model provider have explicitly stated to have trained on. This typically only includes the training split.

Observed a fun fact: English-only models tend to get worse performance on closed datasets, while multilingual models are better at closed dataset.

Sources indicate that is it because the baseline, MTEB, is a benchmark merely in English, and RTEB is multilingual? It's natural that multilingual model get better performance on multilingual benchmark instead of English.

RTEB is by default multilingual, however it has an English subset (at the moment denoted as RTEB(eng, beta) or RTEB English on the leaderboard selection menu).

There is also an argument that multilingual models are more robust to phenomena such as code-switching and foreign terms.

Are you planning on releasing an academic paper on RTEB?

It has been revealed that the discussion about English-only versus multilingual subsets demonstrates why a single retrieval average can hide notable differences. Would it be feasible to report lexical baselines alongside embedding models per language, including identifier-heavy and paraphrase-heavy slices? We recently evaluated BM25 plus semantic reranking on a small English-only workload: https://huggingface.co/blog/ironbcc/bm25-seb-rag-retrieval (I'm an author). That result doesn't tell us how the approach would perform on RTEB's multilingual or private datasets.

RTEB leaderboard have bm25 and some other baseline models https://leaderboard.mteb.org/benchmark/RTEB(beta)?pin=mteb%252Fbaseline-bm25s.

OpenAI releases GPT-6.2 Astra to regain performance lead from Claude Fable 5.2

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the frontier model races continues.
  • According to recent reports, stepping back in time a few days, Anthropic last week launched Claude Fable and Mythos 5.2.
  • OpenAI demonstrates that GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol are more or less playing ball with Anthropic’s latest models, but often delivering similar performance at a drastically lower cost.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the frontier model races continues. A week after the launch of Anthropic’s Claude 5.2 and Google’s Gemini 4 Hydrogen, OpenAI is releasing GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol as a “new standard for professional work.”.

According to recent reports, stepping back in time a few days, Anthropic last week launched Claude Fable and Mythos 5.2. The company’s latest models are “designed to tackle the most daunting technical challenges with “improvements in areas like coding, reasoning, and vision.” Anthropic states that Fable 5.2 beats Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra, and Gemini 4 Carbon virtually across the board in benchmarks including coding, cybersecurity, knowledge work, and more.

But, now, OpenAI is stepping up to the challenge.

OpenAI demonstrates that GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol are more or less playing ball with Anthropic’s latest models, but often delivering similar performance at a drastically lower cost.

Of the two latest models, OpenAI claims that Sol is “smarter, more efficient, and lets you complete more tasks on the same paid strategy” as a “go-to model for everyday work.”.

Astra, meanwhile, is tuned for the highest-quality work in professional use cases such as documents, slides, coding, and more:.

It has been revealed that GPT‑6.2 Astra sets a new quality bar for AI in complex professional work. Its slides, spreadsheets, and documents read less like AI, and more closely follow the templates you provide and the conventions of your field. It writes cleaner code and builds frontends that look and work better, particularly for websites, gaming, and 3D design.

GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol are now available to all Plus, Pro, Enterprise, and Edu customers in ChatGPT Work and Codex, with Astra being significantly more affordable compared to GPT-6 Astra. Pricing for Astra per million tokens lands at $8 for input, $0.40 for cached input, and $40 for output. Sol matches its predecessor at $2 for input, $0.10 for cached input, and $10 for output, again per million tokens.

4 ways I gave my employees more time off without sacrificing results

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2439 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A decade ago, I couldn’t have told you the last time I took significant time off from work.
  • A decade ago, I couldn’t have told you the last time I took significant time off from work.
  • In a recent development, I wore “busy” like a badge of honor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A decade ago, I couldn’t have told you the last time I took significant time off from work. I wore “busy” like a badge of honor. As the business owner, I set the tone for the people on my team. Pushing ourselves to do more and work harder was woven into the fabric of our culture. Today, things could not look more different. Every summer, I take a monthlong vacation to travel with my family. When I work late nights or several days in a row without breaks, I make it up to myself with extra time off. My team gets a four-day workweek and generous PTO, and on top of that, we close our business for six weeks throughout the year and take time off together. And we’ve managed to make this shift without losing sight of high expectations and accountability. What changed? I did. After years of neglecting my health in service of my work, I came across two books that upended my perspective: Dying for a Paycheck by Jeffrey Pfeffer, and It Doesn’t Have to be Crazy at Work by David Heinemeier Hansson and Jason Fried. They highlighted me what my firm’s culture could look like if I took responsibility for changing it. For years now, creating better work-life harmony for me and my team has been my priority. To me, “harmony” means that work and life work together instead of against each other. But of course, it hasn’t been easy. My biggest challenge has been figuring out how to balance caring for my people with creating a sustainable future for my company. I certainly haven’t found all the answers, but several years into this journey, my team and I are able to prioritize our lives outside of work and get stuff done—including writing and launching a upcoming book, just this year. While it’s true that my company and team are significantly smaller than they were in the early days, I believe it’s possible for teams of any size to make shifts that support better work-life harmony. I want to share the biggest things we’ve implemented with the hope that they will spark some ideas of your own. 1. Break weeks Years ago, I took off two separate weeks during a busy time at work. I didn’t have a vacation planned; I just needed a break. When I returned after a week of doing whatever I felt like at home, I felt rejuvenated and inspired. I wanted that same feeling for my team, so I proposed a company-wide “Break Week.” I told the team we would close the business and use the time to recharge. We loved it. Being off at the same time allowed us to disconnect in a way we never had. No one felt like they were falling behind, and we returned with renewed energy. Now, we enjoy six Break Weeks throughout the year: one week at the end of the first three quarters and three at the end of the year. I see them as a way to guarantee that each person on my team—including me—is taking off at least that much time every year. I’ve realized that offering a benefit doesn’t guarantee that people will use it, so implementing a policy like Break Weeks shows my team that I’m serious about time off. You might wonder what our clients think about our closing our business so often, and at first, I worried about that too. I also worried about missing out on revenue. Not only have our clients embraced Break Weeks, but some have even implemented their own version of them. And when we have to turn away revenue, we work to make it up in other quarters. If we can’t, we see it as a reasonable trade-off. 2. Four-day workweeks  Break Weeks were a huge step toward making sure that my team prioritizes their lives outside of work, but for me, it was just the start. When I first proposed the four-day workweek, I knew I’d find it tough to commit to. But as the leader, I needed to model it. I told my team that if I ever had to work all five days, I’d make up for it another time, and I did. Today, I empower each person on my team to choose the day that works best for them to take off each week, and they can change it as needed. To make this work, team communication is critical. We maintain a time-off calendar and share frequent updates on deliverables and deadlines. Once again, I learned that it’s a leader’s job to create a structure that holds everyone accountable to using benefits; otherwise, it just doesn’t happen. 3. Human time off For years, I proudly touted our “unlimited” paid time-off policy. But, of course, there’s only so much time you can take off and expect to remain on payroll. To create better-defined guidelines, I decided to make a distinction between two types of time off: “human” time and vacation time. Human time covers doctor or personal appointments, sick time, mental health days, etc. My team knows that they can take time off for these things without my approval. If human time affects someone’s ability to get their work done, I expect them to communicate that with the team and create a plan. Vacation time, on the other hand, means that you are completely unplugged and unavailable. I ask that my team runs their vacation plans by me before they finalize them so that I can ensure that we’re still meeting the needs of the business. Since I implemented this distinction, I’ve noticed that not only is there more clarity and communication about time off, but the team is taking more of it and working together more proactively. 4. Sabbaticals  This year, I implemented sabbaticals as a way to honor the amount of time my team has chosen to give me and the company. Depending on the person’s tenure, these sabbaticals range from four to six weeks and are fully paid. Each person earns a sabbatical every five years. Because those on my team have been with me for 9, 14, and 15 years, respectively, we are in the process of figuring out the sabbatical schedule so that the needs of the business are still covered. I’m excited to see what we learn and the impact of this new benefit. None of this works without accountability and open communication. We evaluate ourselves and each other’s performance with 360-degree reviews every quarter. We strive to give feedback within 24 hours of an issue’s arising, and we don’t shy away from difficult conversations. If someone isn’t delivering on their results and their time off is affecting their performance, it’s my job to speak up. Since implementing these changes, I’ve noticed my team and I are approaching our work with more energy and enthusiasm. In busy seasons, we’re willing to sprint because we feel taken care of. While some benefits look different for me as the business owner, I’m still taking off more time than ever before. These benefits might sound expensive or over-the-top, but I believe nothing has greater ROI than building a culture where work-life harmony thrives.

To make this work, team communication is critical. We maintain a time-off calendar and share frequent updates on deliverables and deadlines. Once again, I learned that it’s a leader’s job to create a structure that holds everyone accountable to using benefits; otherwise, it just doesn’t happen.

In a recent development, for years, I proudly touted our “unlimited” paid time-off policy. But, of course, there’s only so much time you can take off and expect to remain on payroll. To create better-defined guidelines, I decided to make a distinction between two types of time off: “human” time and vacation time.

Human time covers doctor or personal appointments, sick time, mental health days, etc. My team knows that they can take time off for these things without my approval. If human time affects someone’s ability to get their work done, I expect them to communicate that with the team and create a initiative.

In a recent development, vacation time, on the other hand, means that you are completely unplugged and unavailable. I ask that my team runs their vacation looks by me before they finalize them so that I can ensure that we’re still meeting the needs of the business.

Since I implemented this distinction, I’ve noticed that not only is there more clarity and communication about time off, but the team is taking more of it and working together more proactively.

It has been revealed that this year, I implemented sabbaticals as a way to honor the amount of time my team has chosen to give me and the organization. Depending on the person’s tenure, these sabbaticals range from four to six weeks and are fully paid. Each person earns a sabbatical every five years. Because those on my team have been with me for 9, 14, and 15 years, respectively, we are in the process of figuring out the sabbatical schedule so that the needs of the business are still covered. I’m excited to see what we learn and the impact of this upcoming benefit.

Industry observers note that none of this works without accountability and open communication. We evaluate ourselves and each other’s performance with 360-degree reviews every quarter. We strive to give feedback within 24 hours of an issue’s arising, and we don’t shy away from difficult conversations. If someone isn’t delivering on their results and their time off is affecting their performance, it’s my job to speak up.

Since implementing these changes, I’ve noticed my team and I are approaching our work with more energy and enthusiasm. In busy seasons, we’re willing to sprint because we feel taken care of. While some benefits look different for me as the business owner, I’m still taking off more time than ever before. These benefits might sound expensive or over-the-top, but I believe nothing has greater ROI than building a culture where work-life harmony thrives.

The Razer Basilisk V3 is right now available for a low price of $32.99 on Amazon, down from its regular list price of $69.99. Razer is known to offer some of the best gaming mice on the market, and if you are looking for a latest upgrade, this deal is worth your money. Offering an ergonomic design, the mouse comes with a variety of customizations and can cater to a variety of gaming genres.

The Razer Basilisk V3 is a wired gaming mouse featuring a right-handed design, a textured matte-black finish, and a thumb rest. It features 13 programmable inputs, including the scroll wheel controls, which can be configured for different commands, macros, and shortcuts. The mouse uses Razer's Focus+ optical sensor with a native sensitivity of 20,000 DPI, which can be increased to 26,000 DPI using Razer’s Synapse software. It also has a dedicated sniper button that can temporarily lower sensitivity for more precise aiming.

The Basilisk V3 features  11 programmable buttons via Razer's Synapse software and a multi-function trigger button for keybinding actions such as a push-to-talk button.

One of its main features is the HyperScroll Tilt Wheel, which supports both notched scrolling and a free-spinning mode. It also includes Smart-Reel Mode, which automatically switches to free-spinning when the wheel is scrolled promptly and returns to tactile scrolling at slower speeds. Other features include 11 customizable RGB lighting zones, three polling rate options of 125 Hz, 500 Hz, and 1,000 Hz, and second-generation optical switches. The mouse also features a 6-foot braided USB cable and weighs approximately 94 grams.

Considering its discounted price of $32.99, the Razer Basilisk V3 offers a solid set of features at less than half its original price. Its ergonomic design, customizable buttons, adjustable sensitivity, and versatile scroll wheel make it suitable for both gaming and everyday desktop use.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Meta’s WhatsApp is making a huge change to chat backups, with a new built-in cloud backup option on Android that doesn’t rely on Google, and is free.

Spotted by WABetaInfo, WhatsApp for Android is adding its own cloud backup option. Prior to this, the app relied on Google Drive backup for transferring chats between devices or keeping a backup in case of accidental deletion.

According to recent reports, “WhatsApp cloud storage” is showing up in the WhatsApp for Android v2.26.46.4 beta enhancement, rolling out now, and includes 2GB of free storage for cloud backups. Everything is still end-to-end encrypted. Beyond the first 2GB, WhatsApp Plus ($2.99/month) adds 100GB, and Meta One ($7.99/month+) offers up to 4TB of cloud storage. WhatsApp will keep your backup for at least 4 months after the subscription ends, even if you are over the 2GB gap.

You can still choose to use Google Drive backups instead of the built-in option, but those using devices without a Google account or who are running low on Google storage may appreciate the option to switch.

It’s unclear exactly when this will be available to all WhatsApp users.

A frontend application can compile successfully and still fail when it communicates with the backend.

Imagine a backend developer changes an API response from:.

Recent findings suggest that the backend works correctly. The frontend also builds without errors. However, a component expecting user.name now receives undefined.

This is an example of API contract drift: the frontend and backend no longer agree on the structure or behavior of an API.

Recent findings suggest that the problem becomes more difficult when several developers or teams work on different parts of an application. A change made by one team may affect another team's assumptions without producing an obvious error during development.

It has been revealed that typeScript helps catch many programming mistakes, but its types do not automatically validate data received over HTTP. A type declaration can describe what the application expects without proving that the server actually returns it.

In this tutorial, we'll look at a practical way to make API contracts more reliable.

Consider a typical frontend API function:.

At first glance, this looks reasonable.

The function promises to return a User, so TypeScript allows the application to access properties such as name and email.

It has been revealed that the return value of response.json() is not automatically checked against the User interface. The interface only provides compile-time information; it does not validate the actual JSON received from the server.

the frontend may still treat the response as a User even though the data has a different structure.

This is particularly vital when working with:.

Independently deployed frontend and backend applications.

APIs maintained by different engineering teams.

The solution is to validate data at the boundary where it enters the application.

Industry observers note that zod is a TypeScript-first schema validation library. It allows developers to describe expected data structures and validate actual values against those definitions.

Now create a schema for the user response:.

There are two crucial parts here.

First, UserSchema describes the structure that the application expects at runtime.

Second, z.infer generates the corresponding TypeScript type from the schema.

This means developers do not need to maintain a separate interface and validation definition for the same data structure.

The response is initially treated as unknown, which prevents the application from assuming that untrusted data already has the expected structure.

UserSchema.parse() validates the actual response.

If the backend returns an unexpected property type or misses a required field, Zod throws a validation error instead of allowing invalid data to move silently through the application.

You can also use safeParse() when you prefer to handle validation errors without exceptions:.

This approach is useful when API responses are external or when a frontend must provide more controlled error handling.

One common mistake is placing API validation logic directly inside React components.

Recent findings suggest that for a small application, this may seem convenient. As the project grows, however, it becomes difficult to reuse validation rules and identify where data transformations happen.

A better approach is to separate API schemas, service functions, and UI components.

The responsibilities are straightforward:.

schemas/user.ts defines the expected user data.

api/client.ts handles common HTTP configuration.

api/people.ts contains user-related API requests.

hooks/useUser.ts manages data fetching for React.

components/UserProfile.tsx displays the validated data.

This structure makes it easier to change an API implementation without rewriting the UI.

It also makes testing more manageable because validation logic can be tested independently of React rendering.

For more ideas on organizing application code, see SitePoint's guide to modern JavaScript modules.

Runtime validation protects an application when data arrives. However, teams also need a shared description of what an API is supposed to accept and return.

This is where OpenAPI becomes useful.

OpenAPI provides a standard format for describing HTTP APIs, including:.

Request and response structures.

Data types and validation constraints.

For example, an endpoint can be described using an OpenAPI document:.

This document describes what the endpoint should return.

Both frontend and backend developers can refer to the same contract instead of relying on separate assumptions or outdated documentation.

Swagger Editor helps developers write and validate OpenAPI documents. It also provides a convenient way to inspect API definitions.

Swagger UI turns an OpenAPI document into interactive API documentation, allowing developers to explore endpoints and test requests.

Redoc provides another way to generate readable API documentation from an OpenAPI specification.

These tools are particularly useful when APIs are maintained by multiple developers or consumed by several applications.

Maintaining API types manually across frontend and backend repositories creates opportunities for inconsistencies.

For example, a backend developer might add a latest optional property while the frontend continues using an older interface.

One way to reduce this duplication is to generate TypeScript definitions and API clients from an OpenAPI specification.

Orval is a useful tool for this workflow.

It can generate TypeScript clients and types from an OpenAPI document, helping frontend developers work with consistent endpoint definitions.

A simplified workflow looks like this:.

A typical configuration might look like this:.

The exact configuration depends on the Orval version and the structure of the OpenAPI document.

Once configured, the client can be regenerated when the API specification changes.

This reduces the amount of repetitive code developers need to maintain manually.

However, generated types should not be confused with runtime validation. They improve consistency during development, but an application may still need to validate responses received from external systems or services that cannot be fully trusted.

Frontend developers often need to build or test features before the corresponding backend endpoint is ready.

Waiting for a complete backend implementation can slow down development, particularly when multiple teams work independently.

Mock Service Worker (MSW) helps solve this problem by intercepting network requests and returning controlled responses.

You can define a mock handler for the user endpoint:.

The frontend can now make normal HTTP requests while MSW supplies predictable responses during development or testing.

You can also simulate an invalid response:.

This makes it possible to check whether the application's validation and error-handling logic behave as expected.

MSW is particularly valuable because it allows frontend tests to run without requiring a live backend environment.

Runtime validation and generated clients improve reliability, but they do not automatically guarantee that independently developed services remain compatible.

For systems with multiple services, contract testing can provide another layer of protection.

Pact is a contract-testing tool that allows consumers and providers to verify their expectations about API interactions.

Consider a frontend application that expects the user endpoint to return:.

The consumer defines the expected interaction.

The backend provider can then run verification against that contract to check whether its actual response satisfies the consumer's expectations.

This helps identify breaking changes before they reach production.

Sources indicate that these tools solve different problems. A project does not necessarily need all of them, but larger applications can benefit from combining the approaches that match their architecture.

A contract is only useful if developers consistently check it when making changes.

A practical approach is to run validation and tests automatically whenever someone opens a pull request.

For example, a GitHub Actions workflow might look like this:.

The api:validate script should be configured to validate the project's OpenAPI document or run the relevant contract checks.

The test command should execute the application's automated tests.

For a production project, you may also want to include:.

Generated-client consistency checks.

Consumer-provider contract verification.

The objective is to detect incompatible changes before they are merged.

A failed pipeline gives developers an opportunity to investigate the change while the context is still fresh.

API contracts become harder to maintain when several teams contribute to the same system.

For example, a manufacturer might have separate teams responsible for:.

Customer-facing frontend applications.

If nobody owns an API contract, small changes can create unexpected problems for other teams.

Assigning clear ownership helps establish who reviews changes, maintains documentation, and coordinates breaking updates.

This becomes particularly important when an organization expands its engineering capacity across locations or adds several specialized teams. Companies planning that kind of growth may also need to consider enterprise IT recruitment as part of their wider engineering workforce strategy.

Regardless of how a team is assembled, its development process should establish clear responsibilities for API design, versioning, testing, and release coordination.

A few practical conventions can make a significant difference:.

Assign an owner to every important API or service.

Document breaking changes before implementation.

Require contract-related tests in pull requests.

Keep generated clients synchronized with the API specification.

Communicate deprecations before removing existing fields.

Monitor production errors after deploying API changes.

These practices help prevent a growing engineering organization from becoming a collection of disconnected services.

Industry observers note that API contract drift is not simply a TypeScript problem. It is a coordination problem that becomes visible when applications and services develop different expectations about the same data.

TypeScript provides useful compile-time checks, but it cannot guarantee that an HTTP response matches a declared interface.

A more reliable approach combines several techniques:.

Use Zod to validate incoming data.

Use OpenAPI to document API expectations.

Generate TypeScript clients with tools such as Orval.

Use MSW to test frontend behavior without a live backend.

Use Pact when consumer-provider contract verification is appropriate.

Run validation and tests automatically in CI/CD.

You do not need to introduce every tool at once. Start by validating external API responses, document notable endpoints, and gradually automate contract checks as the application grows.

The result is a codebase where developers can make changes with greater confidence and where frontend and backend teams have a shared understanding of how their systems communicate.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that every year our hardware is a little more powerful, our models a little smarter for each parameter.
  • Enter the Neural Engine, Apple's custom AI accelerator that has shipped with every Apple device since 2017.
  • In a recent development, whilst this all sounds very appealing, unfortunately the Neural Engine is only accessible through Core ML, Apple's closed source ML framework.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that every year our hardware is a little more powerful, our models a little smarter for each parameter. In 2025, it is more feasible than ever to run truly competitive models on-device. dots.ocr, a 3B parameter OCR model from RedNote, surpasses Gemini 2.5 Pro in OmniDocBench, making OCR a truly no compromises on-device use case. Running models on-device is certainly appealing to developers: no smuggling API keys, zero cost, and no network required. However, if we want these models to run on-device, we need to be mindful of the limited compute and power budgets.

Enter the Neural Engine, Apple's custom AI accelerator that has shipped with every Apple device since 2017. This accelerator is designed for high performance whilst sipping battery power. Some of our testing has found the Neural Engine to be 12x more power efficient than CPU, and 4x more power efficient than GPU.

In a recent development, whilst this all sounds very appealing, unfortunately the Neural Engine is only accessible through Core ML, Apple's closed source ML framework. Furthermore, even just converting a model from PyTorch to Core ML can present some challenges, and without a preconverted model or some knowledge of the sharp edges it can be arduous for developers. Luckily, Apple also offers MLX, a more modern and flexible ML framework that targets the GPU (not the Neural Engine), and can be used in conjunction with Core ML.

In this three part series, we will provide a reasoning trace of how we converted dots.ocr to run on-device, using a combination of CoreML and MLX. This process should be applicable to many other models, and we hope that this will help highlight the ideas and tools needed for developers looking to run their own models on-device.

It has been revealed that to follow along, clone the repo. You'll need uv and hf installed to run the setup command:.

If you just want to skip ahead and use the converted model, you can download it here.

Converting from PyTorch to CoreML is a two step process:.

Whilst we do have a few knobs we can tweak for step 2, most of our control is in step 1, the graph we feed to coremltools.

Following the programmers litany of make it work, make it right, make it fast, we will first focus on getting the conversion working on GPU, in FLOAT32, and with static shapes. Once we have this working, we can dial down the precision and try and move to the Neural Engine.

According to recent reports, dots.OCR consists of two key components: A 1.2B parameter vision encoder trained from scratch, based on the NaViT architecture, and a Qwen2.5-1.5B backbone. We will be using CoreML to run the vision encoder, and MLX to run the LM backbone.

In order to convert a model, it's best to understand the structure and function before getting started. Looking at the original vision modelling file here, we can see that the vision encoder is similar to the QwenVL family. Like many vision encoders, the vision encoder for dots works on a patch basis, in this case 14x14 patches. The dots vision encoder is capable of processing videos and batches of images. This gives us an opportunity to simplify by only processing a single image at a time. This approach is frequent in on-device apps, where we convert a model that provides the essential functions and iterate if we want to process multiple images.

Sources indicate that when kicking off the conversion process, it's best to start with a minimal viable model. This means removing any bells and whistles that are not strictly necessary for the model to function. In our case, dots has many different attention implementations available for both the vision encoder and the LM backbone. CoreML has lots of infrastructure oriented around the scaled_dot_product_attention operator, which they introduced in iOS 18. We can simplify the model by removing all of the other attention implementations and just focusing on simple sdpa (not the memory efficient variant) for now, commit here.

Once we've done this, we see a scary warning message when we load the model:.

The model doesn't require Sliding Window Attention to function, so we can happily move on.

Recent findings suggest that using torch.jit.trace is still the most mature method for converting models to CoreML. We usually encapsulate this in a simple harness that allows you to modify the compute units used and the precision selected.

You can check out the initial harness here. If we run the following on the original code implementation:.

Sources indicate that luckily this error gives us quite a bit of information. We can look at the VisionRotaryEmbedding layer and see the following code:.

After fixing this, running the conversion again leads us to our next issue at repeat_interleave:.

Whilst this error is less informative, we only have a single call to repeat_interleave in our vision encoder:.

Industry observers note that cu_seqlens is used for masking variable length sequences in flash_attention_2. It's derived from the grid_thw tensor, which represents time, height and width. Since we are only processing a single image, we can simply remove this call, commit here.

Industry observers note that onto the next! This time, we get a more cryptic error:.

This is again due to the masking logic to handle variable length sequences. Since we are only processing a single image (not a video or batch of images), we don't really need attention masking at all! Therefore, we can just use a mask of all True. To prepare ourselves for the Neural Engine conversion, we also switch from using a boolean mask to a float mask of all zeros, as the Neural Engine does not support bool tensors commit here.

It has been revealed that with all of this done, the model should now successfully convert to CoreML! However, when we run the model, we get the following error:.

This reshape could be in multiple places! Luckily, we can use a previous warning message to help us track down the issue:.

Most ML compilers do not like dynamic control flow. Luckily for us, as we are only processing a single image, we can simply remove the loop and process the single h, w pair, commit here.

According to recent reports, and there we have it! If we run the conversion again, we should see that the model successfully converts and matches the original PyTorch precision:.

Now that we've got the model working, let's evaluate the size and performance. The good news is the model is working, the bad news is that it's over 5GB! This is completely untenable for on device deployment! To benchmark the computation time, we can use the built in XCode tooling by calling:.

In a recent development, over a second for a single forward pass of the vision encoder! We have lots of more work.

In the second part of this series, we will work on the integration between CoreML and MLX, to run the full model on-device. In the third part, we will dive deep into the optimizations required to get this model running on the Neural Engine, including quantization and dynamic shapes.

  • It’s a grim milestone for the popular burger chain as it works to execute on a turnaround strategy aimed at boosting sales and bolstering its brand image.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The owner of a dwindling empire of Wendy’s restaurants on Friday disclosed its plans to close several more stores, bringing its total number of shuttered locations to almost 100. It’s a grim milestone for the popular burger chain as it works to execute on a turnaround blueprint aimed at boosting sales and bolstering its brand image. The franchisee behind the closures, Meritage Hospitality Group of Grand Rapids, Michigan, is among the largest operators within the Wendy’s system, at one time owning roughly 375 locations across 15 states. It closed dozens of those restaurants in the months before a Chapter 11 bankruptcy filing in September, and has since shuttered additional waves of stores at regular intervals as part of cash collateral agreements with its lenders. How many Wendy’s stores has Meritage closed? According to court documents, Meritage has closed well over 90 Wendy’s locations since late last year, with many of those stores shuttered before its September bankruptcy petition. As is typical in Chapter 11 cases, Meritage is seeking to reject the leases on many of the stores that it closed pre-bankruptcy—roughly 60, court filings show—a list that includes a handful of Taco John’s and Morning Belle locations, in addition to Wendy’s. Since the bankruptcy, Meritage has also closed at least 41 additional Wendy’s restaurants, including six closures that were disclosed on Friday. The newly shuttered restaurants were located in Florida, Georgia, Michigan, and Ohio: 12135 Lem Turner Road Jacksonville, FL 32218 1928 Hwy 155 McDonough, GA 30252 3675 Cascade Road Atlanta, GA 30331 9556 US 31 So Interlochen, MI 49643 8258 Broadmoor Avenue Caledonia, MI 49316 914 Conant St. Maumee, OH 43537 Prior to the above six restaurants, Meritage disclosed waves of store closures on at least five separate occasions: 5 locations on September 25 5 locations on October 2 10 locations on October 9 13 stores on October 16 2 stores on October 30 Fast Company has reached out to Meritage Hospitality Group and Wendy’s for comment. What will happen to Meritage’s remaining stores? Meritage has owned Wendy’s restaurants since the late 1990s, but its relationship with the fast food giant appeared to turn increasingly contentious in recent years as its business faced headwinds on numerous fronts, including the soaring cost of beef. The franchisee has blamed Wendy’s for a strategy of “deep discounting” that it says squeezed profits. The Wendy’s Company, for its part, had sought to terminate Meritage’s franchise agreements, claiming to be owed more than $146 million in past-due royalties and other fees. Despite all this animosity, the two sides are working together to salvage what’s left of the Meritage fleet. Wendy’s disclosed earlier this month that it wants to buy up to 163 restaurants from Meritage. That deal, which is still subject to better bids, is expected to close early next year. Additionally, Meritage is moving to sell restaurants to various other buyers in separate deals, including one to sell 42 locations in Arkansas, Mississippi, Missouri, and Tennessee to an entity called Divine Infinity Operations. It’s unclear if additional Wendy’s locations could close before or after these asset sales are complete. This story is developing….

  • Amazon is extending that sale to a variety of bundles it has available.
  • This bundle includes the Nintendo Switch 2 console, a code for Mario Kart World, and three months of a Nintendo Switch Online Individual membership.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nintendo raised the price of the Switch 2 earlier this year in response to rising NAND and DRAM prices, but on Black Friday, you can wipe out that hike with a variety of bundles available on Amazon. The core deal is the Mario Kart World Switch 2 bundle, which includes the game, the console, and three months of Nintendo Switch Online. It normally sells for $550, but Amazon has it marked down by $50, bringing the bundle down to its original price of $499.

Amazon is extending that sale to a variety of bundles it has available. You can pick up the kit alongside a Switch 2 Pro Controller, the upcoming Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake, or a microSD Express card with the same discount. Note that with the base Mario Kart World bundle, the game is included as a redeemable code, not a physical cartridge.

This bundle includes the Nintendo Switch 2 console, a code for Mario Kart World, and three months of a Nintendo Switch Online Individual membership.

As you can read about in our Nintendo Switch 2 review published last year, the console is a major upgrade over the original version. The heart of the handheld is a custom Nvidia SoC that includes eight Arm Cortex-A78C CPU cores alongside an Nvidia GPU with 1,536 CUDA cores, hailing from the firm's Ampere generation. Alongside the SoC, the handheld sports 12GB of LPDDR5X memory along with 256GB of storage.

Showing off the capabilities of these upgraded internals is a larger 7.9-inch, 1080p LCD display. It's larger and brighter than the original Switch display, but it also comes with far greater capabilities, including variable refresh rate, HDR10 support, and a 120 Hz panel.

Sources indicate that the handheld is much larger overall, and it sports a redesigned Joy-Con mechanism that's far more resilient than the original Switch design. The kickstand more closely aligns with the Switch OLED, running along most of the edge of the display; the original Switch props up the console on one side, where it can easily fall over.

Sources indicate that overall, the performance jump is what stands out most. Nintendo has released several Switch 2 updates for flagship titles like Metroid Prime 4 and The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom with support for higher resolutions and frame rates. Titles like the recent Ocarina of Time Remake and Donkey Kong Bananza target 60 FPS, though occasionally fall short of that mark.
